en: Having bowed to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and the true gurus beginning with Pūrṇabodha,
I compose the Bhāvadīpa, a commentary on the purport of the Gītā.

At the beginning of the work, he performs an auspicious invocation in the form of a prostration to the Blessed Lord, who is the sole master of all speech, mind, deities, and senses. Regarding the verse beginning with "Indire" (O Mother Indirā): this is not for the sake of his own excellence, but rather for the purpose of obtaining His grace; it is with this intention that he says "amanda... and so forth. To dispel the doubt—arising from the scriptural statement "The Self is bodiless and consists of pure consciousness"—as to how one who is bodiless can be a "royal swan in the lotus-face," he says "sundarākṛtayaḥ" (of beautiful form). The sense is that the scripture is intended to negate a material body.

He bows to the authors of the treatises: "Dharma... [and so on]. The plural number is used because of their greatness; the same applies hereafter. He supplicates the authors of the ancient commentaries: "May that Padmanābha... Just as the mass of the sun's rays serves for the enlightenment of the world, may the collection of these [sages'] words serve for my enlightenment. Two meanings are to be understood in the second half of the verse as well. In the reading *śrīpadmanābha*, because of the hearing of the word *yat* ("that"), it should be construed as "that mass of rays. Having bowed to his own guru, named Akṣobhyatīrtha, he declares his intention to compose [the work]: "Having prostrated... and so forth.

Regarding the word *atha*: it signifies "commencement," meaning that the commentary on each section of the text is now begun. The statement regarding the "seed" (*bīja*) in the commentary refers to the phrase "entirely," and so forth. The phrase "by others" and so forth is stated to establish the meaning of the term "properly. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "completion, etc.," the accumulation [of merit] is included. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "succession, etc.," there is the inclusion of the Vedic injunction inferred from that: "One desiring the completion of what is about to be undertaken should perform obeisance to one's chosen deity. The statement regarding the purpose of the composition is "for the sake of the disciples";
the meaning is that this must necessarily be performed even by the disciples, in order to inform them of this.

He states that there is no tautology by means of the entire phrase: "sampūrṇam" (complete). Regarding "in the well-known Gītās," the meaning is: in those consisting of the *Veṇugītā*, *Bhramaragītā*, *Gopikāgītā*, *Bhikṣugītā*, and so forth.

Regarding "of that very [work]," it should be construed as: "by excluding either the *Mahābhārata* itself or other texts contained within it. With the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely), he provides the answer by stating the purport of the first and second halves of the verse beginning with "śāstreṣu" (in the scriptures), starting with "bhāratasya" (of the *Mahābhārata*).

Regarding the representative, such as a stone and so forth: he states that its "largeness" (*mahattvam*) is the cause of its weight. He says, "Because of its largeness, and because it is stretched by that very weight. From "largeness" (*mahattvāt*), there is "great weight" (*mahābhāraḥ*). Precisely because of this etymological derivation (*niruktatvāt*), it should be understood as a compound ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī-samāsa*). Because it is "stretched" (*tatatvāt*), meaning pervaded, by that great weight—this is the sense: the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *tan* with the word "great weight" (*mahābhāra*) as a prefix. "Etymological derivation" (*nirvacanam*) means the explanation of the meaning of the individual parts of a word.

Keeping in mind what was said by the sages to Pṛthu, beginning with "This [form] is a portion (kalā) of the Blessed Viṣṇu, the purifier of the worlds," he raises an objection: "In the case of Pṛthu and others. By the word "others" (ādi), Balarāma, Kārtavīryārjuna, and so forth are included. With the thought that these individuals do not possess the status of being direct incarnations (avatāras)—based on such statements as "The four-armed God, bearing the conch and discus, entered Pṛthu" and "Pṛthu, Haihaya, and others were souls; Hari Himself entered into them"—he explains the meaning of the word "Himself" (svayam).
"Directly Nārāyaṇa," and "Secret"—these two expressions are explicit in the second chapter of the *Bhāratatātparya*, as well as in other Purāṇas.

The introduction (*upoddhāta*): "Intending to favor [him]"—the sense is that since people desire elaboration when something has been stated briefly, the failure to generate a desire for knowledge even through elaboration is the root [of the problem] here. "The word *iti* is a supplement"—the meaning is that after the word *nārāyaṇa*, the word *iti* is mentioned, and the word *ucyate* (is said) is to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). "From this traditional teaching (*smṛti*)"—the meaning is from the *Bhāgavata* tradition: "By knowledge he sustains me. Here, regarding the state of being a knower (*jñānitva*).

The sense is that this is according to the Smṛti: "Those who have not attained the state of the gods are devoid of the vision of Brahman. Regarding the phrase "in this very [context]": the meaning is "only in the suppression of the enemy and his followers. Regarding the phrase "of some": the sense is that this refers to Duryodhana and others, because Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others are their followers. Regarding the phrase "by one learned in the scriptures": the meaning is by Arjuna. Regarding the phrase "a single portion of dharma": this refers to the form of battle; whereas complete dharma consists of one's prescribed livelihood, devotion to the Lord, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "it is indeed combined": [this means it is joined with other duties].

The meaning is that one's own prescribed mode of livelihood, preceded by devotion, dispassion, and so forth, is the supreme dharma. Since even withdrawal from battle is indeed adharma because it is contrary to the supreme dharma, its instruction must also certainly be carried out; this is the meaning. "Because of being such" means because of the state of being dharma or adharma. If [the opponent] were to argue that even what is contrary to that becomes dharma if it is regulated as dharma, he says: "And of that... [to refute this].

The meaning is that it is logically consistent to define *dharma* and *adharma* precisely as those actions performed by one’s own prescribed occupation (*svavihitavṛtti*) preceded by devotion to Hari, and those of a nature contrary to that [occupation]. Regarding the phrase "of the aforementioned kind": this means of the worship of the Lord being performed through one's own prescribed occupation preceded by devotion. With the intention that the reason for its being a duty is obtained from the fourth quarter [of the verse], he says "mokṣa... (referring to the word *mokṣa*). He states "hita... and so forth, having obtained the reasons from the two phrases "this is for your benefit" and "you shall come to Me alone. And regarding the phrase "the state of being abandoned": [this refers to the abandonment of what is contrary to the aforementioned].

The word "is understood" (*avagamyate*) should be supplied [to complete the sentence]. He clarifies this with the passage beginning with "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*). By way of restating the phrase "by one's own duty" (*svadharmeṇa*), he states the remainder: "and by devotion" (*bhaktyā ca*) should be joined [to the previous statement]. If it is asked, "How is this meaning—that worship of the Lord alone is *dharma* (duty) and that which is contrary to it is *adharma*—obtained from this? he replies: "It is to be performed" (*kartavya*). If it is asked, "On what basis is devotion intended in the *Gītā* as the supreme *dharma*? he connects the root text: "Beyond the senses" (*parokṣa*).

The meaning is that, because it is understood that [liberation] depends upon devotion—given that "to know" and "to see" refer respectively to the indirect and direct [realizations], and "to enter" refers to the liberation of the knower—it is stated, "by means of exclusive devotion. Regarding the phrase "otherwise": this means if knowledge were dependent solely on hearing and so forth. He states the meaning of the root text as a response to an objection: "of hearing and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of its being the highest": thus the Sūtra says, "And by the subsequent word, there is the same nature [as the previous]; but the connection [to the former] is due to abundance. "Therein" refers to...

The meaning of the verse "all dharmas" (*sarvadharmān*) is that there is an intended absence of both what is to be performed and what is to be abandoned. The intention of the objector is that, due to the absence of anything to be rejected or accepted, his [the Lord's] purpose is solely the taking of refuge. Alternatively, it should be understood that the word *tatra* (there) means "in the Gītā. To explain how these two points are understood from the verse "one who performs my work, for whom I am the supreme" (*matkarmakṛnmatparama*), he clarifies them under the guise of a restatement, beginning with "that which was said," etc. Having stated the meaning of the term *gītā*, he explains the meaning of the root word *tat-karma*: "that very thing is *tat-karma*. This indicates that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

The meaning is that for the devotee, even action directed toward objects other than the Blessed Lord is itself "action" [in the sense of being bondage]; the meaning is that because it is performed for His sake—that is, for the sake of the Blessed Lord—it is indeed prohibited. "Therein" means in the *Gītā*. Manifesting this, he states the meaning of the root text: "prescribed by oneself. It has already been stated that the word "is understood" (*avagamyate*) is to be supplied everywhere. The phrase "both of those" means "that which is prescribed by oneself and that which is for the sake of the Blessed Lord. "By this" means by this half-verse.

"Directly or indirectly": [the attributes] ending with "by virtue of being faultless" are required directly; however, for the others, they are required indirectly. This is because, if the object were non-different from itself, devoid of its own nature, or superior to itself, it would be impossible for it to exercise control over all things—both eternal and spatial—given that it is itself devoid of qualities such as omniscience and omnipotence, and possessed of defects such as birth and death. Furthermore, if it were dependent on another, then, in the absence of that other's consent, through the agency of its own will and so forth, it could not be the cause of liberation for another by means of bestowing the goals of human existence.

The sense is that even the status of being what is propounded by the scripture—namely, the making known of injunctions and prohibitions, or the regulation [of beings] through means such as meditation—is not something that must be produced [as an effect]. "Everything is dependent on Him" refers to the phrase "the Great Lord of the world. "Intellect" refers to the statement "everything is dependent on Him," based on the supplementary passage: "The various states of beings arise from Me alone."

Having begun with "The seven sages," [the Lord] says: "He who knows this glory and yoga of Mine in truth, he is joined to unshakable yoga; there is no doubt in this. Because of hearing this remainder of the statement, He says: "Unshakable" (*niṣkampa*). Adopting the derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa*), He says: "Of all the scriptures" (*sarvaśāstrāṇām*). Since the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "higher knowledge" (*vijñāna*) refer to the subject matter of the scriptures, how is their reference to the Blessed One obtained? To this, He says: "Of the Blessed One" (*bhagavad-*)—meaning, because it was stated in the half-verse beginning with "Having known which" (*yajjñātvā*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that since it is stated in passages such as "by which the unheard becomes heard" that everything is known through the knowledge of the Blessed One, and since here it is stated that [everything] is known through the knowledge [of Him] in the passage beginning with "having known which, there is nothing more here," it is established that all scriptures have the Blessed One as their ultimate subject. "The statement regarding preeminence" refers to the intention that the term *rājavidyā* (royal science) is explained as the "preeminent science. "Liberation from that knowledge" refers to the intention expressed in the statement, "I am the foundation of absolute bliss."

Because of the statement "another," he says: "Difference. Because of the statement "the highest," he says: "The state of being the highest has been stated. Because of the statement "He sustains," he says: "Everything is dependent on Him. Because of the statement "Renowned in the world and in the Veda," he says: "Of all the scriptures. Because of the statements "He is wise" and "He has accomplished all that was to be done," he says: "Liberation [results] from knowledge of Him. Regarding the phrase "To them, it is unreal and without foundation": the sense is that by censuring those who maintain such views as unreality and so forth, the reality of the world is understood. As for what was said: [text follows].

The meaning is that, having cited such statements as "Perform action," it was stated that even for the knower (*jñānin*), there is action for the sake of the Lord. [The phrase] "to be accomplished by the knower" means that he too must strive for it. [The expression] "due to the lack of certainty regarding liberation" refers to the intent of the sūtra: "There is no restriction for all. He says "by him" with the understanding that "therefore" is the ellipsis; the meaning is "by means of action appropriate to one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). [The phrase] "or from that" means that the word "therefore" is to be construed with the statement "one should perform action."

Regarding the phrase "the state of being the supreme means" (*sādhanottamatvam*), etc.: by the word "etc. (*ityādi*), it is understood that even for one who possesses indirect or direct knowledge, liberation is dependent upon that [devotion]. Regarding the statement "it is said": the meaning is that it is stated by the verse, "The Supreme Lord, pleased by devotion, bestows knowledge. Regarding "of hearing and so forth" (*śravaṇādeḥ*): the intention is [as taught] in such passages as, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*). Regarding "liberation and so forth" (*mokṣādiḥ*): the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has "knowledge" (*jñāna*) as its referent.

Regarding the statement, "Vision and so forth are its means," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes meditation (*dhyāna*) and hearing (*śravaṇa*). Furthermore, by the word "its" (*tasya*), one should understand that the threefold affection—namely, the immature, the mature, and the fully matured—that was described as the meaning of the term *bhakti*, is all included. Having accepted this, [the author], in order to show through discrimination which among vision and the rest is the means for which specific form of affection (*sneha*), addresses the doubt raised in the verse beginning with "How is devotion... (*kathaṃ bhakteḥ*) and so on.

By the words "extremely mature" (*atiparipakva*) and so forth: *yoga* means the means (*upāya*). "Because it is the means for that" means because it is the means for devotion that is extremely mature, which itself is the means for liberation. "The means for that" means the means for devotion that is mature through the means of [right] vision (*dṛṣṭi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "hearing and so forth," reflection (*manana*) is included. "As has been stated" means as was cited in the passage beginning with "This form is very difficult to see."

It should be understood that the statement, "The status of being a deity implies the highest qualification," is a restatement (anuvāda) made in accordance with his own previous exposition. Regarding the phrase "and in the case of pervasion" (vyāptau): the sense is that the author intends the pervasion (vyāpti) expressed in the root text as "those who are deities are the highest qualified. Regarding the phrase "that which belongs to Viṣṇu": the meaning is that this was stated after citing such passages as "There is none equal to you. *Mīlaḥ* means one who sprinkles what is desired; *eṣasya* means of the one who rules (*īśa*) everywhere; *vayāḥ* means a binder; *prabharaṇe* refers to worship; and regarding *rudriye*, the suffix *gha* is applied to the word *rudra*, thus forming *raudram*.

*Vide vivide*: from the root *vid-lṛ* in the sense of "obtaining" (*lebha*), meaning "he obtained. The phrase "as it was" (*yathā tathā*) is an elliptical statement. From the hearing of the word *yāsiṣṭam*, the meaning is "you two. *Irāvat* means "possessing food" (*annavat*). *Vartiḥ* means "dwelling" (*vartanam*). The sense is that the suffix *ikāra* is added to the root *vṛt* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). *Yāsiṣṭam* [is read as] *ayāsiṣṭam*; the absence of the augment *aṭ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The meaning is "you two have arrived. To the question "How did he reflect? he himself says: "May these [beings] mentioned below be born. He states the literal meaning of the Vedic words.

"Truth is primary," and "therefore from Viṣṇu. "By measure" means by the measurement of each measure. "Increasing with body" means you are full by your very form. "Others" is an elliptical statement; they "follow after" (anvaśnuvanti)—the root *aś* meaning to pervade—meaning they attain [it]. "As has been said" means as stated in the passage beginning with "Even though seeing this Self," and so forth. "The preceding and following" refers to the fact that the liberated one is the subject under discussion here in the verse beginning, "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi?"

The meaning is that this is because the word "liberated" (mukta) is heard in the subsequent verse, "There is no purpose served by his actions," and [the present statement] follows from that. According to the Bhāṣya, he states that here the word "liberated" refers to one who is established in meditative absorption (samādhi): "In every way here. Some say that because of the word "even" (api) in the phrase "even one established in meditative absorption," the verse refers to two meanings. He states the purport of the phrase "by the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas": "By knowledge alone. The meaning of "for the Sāṅkhyas" is "for the possessors of knowledge" (jñānin). He raises an objection: "Not here."

Regarding the phrase "as has been stated": this means that by the passage beginning with "This form is very difficult to see," it was stated that Arjuna is a man of knowledge (*jñānin*). This concludes the brief statement of the essential meaning of the *Gītā*.

"By the summary statement alone" means by the passage beginning with "In that regard, the direct incarnation of Indra," and so forth. "By the passage beginning with 'Having seen this'... means that in the previous chapter, by the passage beginning with "O Kṛṣṇa, having seen these kinsmen," the justification for withdrawing from battle—namely, fear, trembling, and the loosening of the Gāṇḍīva bow—has already been stated. He takes up the second half [of the verse]; the meaning is clear. The intention is that the word *ca* (and) should be understood as having the sense of a comparison (*upamā*). "It is true."

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: [the Lord] offers an alternative analysis in order to set aside Arjuna’s statement, "I will not fight," which was made out of fear for the destruction caused by affection for his kinsmen. Regarding the word *tat* (that): it means Arjuna’s speech of the aforementioned form. In order to dispel the misconception that the phrase "in this very way" (*evameva*) refers to [Arjuna’s] being the supreme conscious being (*paramacetanatvena*), he says: "as mere consciousness" (*cetanamātratvena*). The sense is that [the Lord is] eternal in the highest degree, as in the passage: "He is the conscious one among the conscious. Regarding the term *vivakṣitā* (intended): [it refers to the intended meaning].

The object [of the two absences] consists in the absence of existence by way of its own nature and by way of the body, [respectively], during the states of prior non-existence and destruction. "Of both kinds" means by way of its own nature and by way of the body. With the intention that the removal of doubt is achieved through the force of citing the specific terms [of the verse], he says: "By the word 'tu'. He states the meaning intended by the word "loka" with the words beginning "prāpta... (attained, etc.). By this—namely, by stating the occasion for the world—he means that there is no contradiction in saying that [the world] was not the subject under discussion from Arjuna's perspective. "Saraṇam" means going.

[The word "sū" is derived from] the verbal root *sū* meaning "to go. The sense is that whatever has the meaning of "going" also has the meaning of "knowing. [Objection: Since the doubt regarding the subject at hand is not resolved by the mere statement, "There is no non-existence of that which exists," [the author] says: "The example. [Regarding] "the latter half": the sense is that by stating in the latter half—namely, "The end of both of these has been seen by the seers of reality"—that "neither pleasure nor pain arises from good or evil deeds," the certainty of this conclusion is obtained through the declaration that the final determination (*anta*) of these two points has been perceived by those who see the truth.

He states what is relevant to the present context: "By lack of faith" (*aśraddhayā*). The meaning is that one should include the verse from the eighteenth chapter, "Whatever is offered, given, or performed as penance without faith, O Pārtha, is called *asat*," along with the sentence occurring slightly after "the word *sat*, O Pārtha, is appropriate. Regarding "one who knows" (*vettā*): the root *vid* means "to know"; thus, the sense is "one who has known. The augment *iṭ* is not applied here because the rule governing grammatical operations (*āgama-śāsana*) is non-mandatory (*anitya*). Now, it might be argued that one should have said "of the existing and the non-existing" (*vidyamānāvidyamānayoḥ*).

Since the word *vidyamāna* (existing) would have been placed first according to the rule "the shorter [word] comes first" (*alpāctaraṃ pūrvaṃ*), and likewise, because existence is more venerable than non-existence, it would have been placed first according to the rule "the more venerable [comes] first" (*abhyarhitaṃ pūrvaṃ*), he says: "In accordance with the Gītā," [and] "origination and destruction. This means: by the conventional usage of origination for that which was non-existent, and the conventional usage of destruction for that which is existent. [The opponent asks: "What is this?"

The meaning is: is the knowledge arising from inference, scripture, or presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), which constitutes the very basis for the conventional usage of the term "neck" (kaṇṭha), a valid cognition or an error? "Ghaṭitam" means: it has been interpreted otherwise by taking it as referring to both existent and non-existent action. "Tau" means: the two, namely, cognition and conventional usage. Immediately after the phrase "therefore, the non-existent is not born," he states the remainder: "the existent does not perish"; thus the conclusion should be understood. "Kimiti" means: what is the purpose of the statement? "By way of a distinction of form" (rūpabhedena).

The meaning is that there is the birth of that which exists in the form of an effect [but] exists in the form of a cause. "Why is this so? means: why is it that there is the birth of the non-existent and the destruction of the existent? "Of the object of error" means: by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) in the form of the inexplicability of appearance and sublation (*khyāti-bādha*) regarding nacre-silver and the like. "In the former position" means: another refutation consisting of the absence of proof against the position that the non-existent is not perceived as non-existent. He states the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*): "not only. "Its attribute" (*taddharma*).

The meaning is: "the property whose nature is being perceived. "Its existence also" means: "the existence of the perception of the non-existent as being existent. "Of the subverting cognition also" means: because of the arising of the opponent's subverting cognition [which holds that] the form perceived in scripture is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) and not even conventionally real (*vyāvahārika-sat*). "Because of the contradiction with indeterminability" means: because it is impossible for that which is the locus of a reality consisting of true existence to be distinct from the non-existent (*sad-vailakṣaṇya*). The meaning of *maghavānau* is "the two glorious ones."

Regarding the statement "yaśo vā va magham," the word *magha* is declared in the Śruti to mean "glory" (*yaśas*) in the context of determining the ritual action. In the verse "acchendrābrahmaṇaspatī," he states "Indra and Bṛhaspati," accepting that the meaning of the term *brahmaṇaspati* is Bṛhaspati. It should have been "indrābṛhaspatī," because the rule "devatādvandve ca" prescribes the substitution of *naṅ* for the first member of the compound. He explains the meaning of the remainder of the verse, "yuvoridāpaścana praminanti vrataṃ vām," with the words beginning "of you two."

"Of you two" means "of both of you. The word *it* has this very meaning. The word *vrata* means "truth," and so forth. The meaning of the two words *āpaścanā* is "even all the deities. They "perceive" means they "know. Having first stated the meaning of the remaining portion—"That [gift] is not in vain; it is desirable wealth; moreover, he shall conquer and give"—he states the meaning of the words already mentioned as "the All-Knowing One. "That must be done" means that the act of battle must be performed.

The verb "will say" (*vakṣyati*) is connected with the phrase "having said" (*uktvā*), as he will state immediately thereafter in the verse beginning "Therefore, meditate upon Him" (*tasmād dhyasva*) that [the meditation] must be performed as an act of worship. "Of both" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Regarding the phrase "of the soul here": the commentary on this verse, which states that the soul's status as the subject to be propounded and its status as the object to be negated are intended, is not meant in a primary sense. To the question, "Why is there a lack of primacy if the soul were the intended subject? he says: "Therein. This means: in Hari.

If it is argued that this verse should therefore refer primarily to Viṣṇu, he says: "But not even I... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "by adding the word 'etcetera'": the meaning is "by the word 'etcetera' such as 'the loss of the body' and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in some way": the meaning is the postulation of a difference in meaning based on the distinction between natural destruction and occasional (accidental) destruction. Regarding the phrase "it is said here": the meaning is "in this work called *Tātparya-nirṇaya*. Regarding the phrase "but in the Bhāṣya": [it is as follows].

The meaning is that by the words "nor is there the destruction of the one who possesses attributes," and so forth, another meaning in the form of the individual soul (jīva) is being stated. "By the Blessed One" means by the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakṛt). "Having stated the absence of insentience" refers to the sense of the passage beginning with "it does not exist," and so forth. "Regarding the body" should be understood as referring to the passage beginning with "dark-complexioned and bright-complexioned. "Of these two sentences" means of the two sentences, "he who knows" and "consisting of bliss," because they belong to the context of the Supreme Brahman as stated in "by knowing Brahman, he attains the Supreme."

"By means of the form of Yaśas" means by means of the form named Yaśas, according to the Vedic text: "His name is Great Glory" (*tasya nāma mahadyaśaḥ*). "By the Lord" is to be construed with "as a friend. He states the meaning of the remainder of the verse, beginning with "Since he," in reference to the passage: "The one who touches away the sin, the father, the winner of wealth—he indeed hastens forward for the prize" (*kilbiṣaspṛtpitupaṇirhyeṣāmaraṃhito bhavati vājināya*). He states the meaning of the remainder of the verse, beginning with "Someone," in reference to the passage: "One sings the *gāyatra* among the *śakvarī* verses; another speaks the sacred word (*brahman*) possessing all knowledge; and another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice" (*gāyatraṃ tvo gāyati śakvarīṣu | brahmā tvo vadati jātavidyāṃ yajñasya mātrāṃ vimita u tvaḥ*).

Regarding the root *jakṣ* (from the sense of eating and laughing), he states the two meanings of the word *jakṣan*: "eating" and "laughing. Regarding the phrase "in those swift as thought," its meaning is "in qualities such as knowledge. He states the meaning of the remainder of the verse—"some reaching to the mouth, some to the armpits, and others appearing like deep lakes after bathing"—with the words "there, some... and "having heard Viṣṇu..."
Having heard Viṣṇu, they have attained the fruit of their ears and are thus endowed with hearing;
and those Gaṇas who, possessing eyes, have seen Viṣṇu, are indeed liberated.
And the gradation among them is clearly declared in the Śruti:
some who have attained liberation remain as curds within the ocean of milk.
Some have arrived at the forest of Brahmā, some at the circle of the Aśvattha tree,
some at Lake Aira, and some gods indeed always [reside] with Hari.
Releasing their coils, they gazed upon him with exceeding joy;
for they behold Viṣṇu, who dwells in the ocean and other abodes, only on rare occasions.

The meaning is: "by the scripture (āgama) stated in the Aitareya Bhāṣya. "For this very reason" means: precisely because of the explanation that the meaning of this sentence has been stated in such a way by the scripture. In order to subsequently analyze the meaning of the sentence "But where [there is] for him," he himself states the passage to be explained by the authority beginning with "name" (saṃjñā), starting with "a mass of consciousness" (prajñānaghana). "To the end of delusion" means to the destruction called delusion. By the phrase ending with "thus" (iti), there is a summary of the passage beginning with "impelled" (codita). "Worldly ignorance" means knowledge consisting of mental modifications (vṛttijñāna).

"In this regard, the meaning is 'one whose object is liberated' (muktaviṣaya). With the intention that the meaning of [the passage] beginning with 'You should ask about that instruction' (tamādeśamaprākṣyaḥ) is [given by the passage] beginning with 'This is Nārāyaṇa,' he says: 'It is that which is instructed' (ādiśyata iti). The meaning is 'the object of instruction. Even in its absence—meaning even in the absence of knowledge of anything else—he states another meaning for [the passage] beginning with 'In which': 'Those which are unknown' (avijñātāni). Thus, 'even of that which is unknown' means even of that which is unknown as being dependent on the Lord and so forth. He speaks in accordance with the expression 'of the knower and so forth' (jñātādeḥ)."

"Known and so forth" (*jñātādi*) refers to the meaning of the words "heard," "thought," and so on. The phrase "it has been stated here" connects with the word "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*). He states the meaning of the Śruti passage, "A mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*), by means of the words beginning with "because. The meaning of the word "real" (*satyam*) is "eternal" (*nityam*). Now he states the meaning of the root text (*mūla*) by means of the words beginning with "on account of its predominance. "Its fruit" is the fruit of conventional knowledge and so forth. To the question "What is that? he says: "The knower," etc. "By that alone" means by conventional knowledge alone.

Thus, having first accepted the grammatical connection that "the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) is the primary one (pradhāna)," he subsequently states the remainder beginning with "Therefore, He is the primary one" (*pradhāno'ta*). Regarding the word "stated" (*uktā*): the meaning is that by the two aforementioned modes, the fruit which belongs to the unknown ignorance and so forth occurs even in their absence; likewise, the fruit which belongs to the known ignorance and so forth also occurs only when the knowledge of the Lord and so forth has arisen. He then states what is to be conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [He is] the primary one" (*pradhānaśca*).

Thus, it should be understood that [the world] is similar [to Brahman]. He states the utility of the portion [of the verse] beginning with "it is the cause" as follows: "precisely its primacy. Furthermore, the similarity between Brahman and the world has been clearly established elsewhere in works such as the *Tattvanirṇaya* through arguments such as "because it is uncontradicted," and so forth; therefore, the intention is that it is not established here.

And thus, regarding both the illustration of "the beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) and the illustration of the lump of clay and its earthen products, the corresponding points of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) have been stated respectively as "thus [is the world] in the Pradhāna" and "thus [is it] similar [to the cause]. Regarding the phrase "in the manifestation of being" (*bhāvākaraṇe*): the meaning is that Uddālaka spoke of the majesty consisting of being the cause of the world, independence, and so forth, in the manifestation of Śvetaketu as a portion of the Lord (*īśvara*). Regarding the phrase "another explanation": this should be construed as being in comparison to his own explanation of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

The meaning of the phrase "the scriptural passage beginning with *tat*," etc., is as follows: the connection [of the words] is that those two cited passages are now being explained. To the question, "How can something not previously taken up by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) be explained? it is said: "[it is] included by the word *ādi* (etc. in the expression 'contradiction with scriptural passages beginning with... Regarding the phrase "in another place": the meaning is "in another scriptural passage," namely, "the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), auspicious, non-dual. And regarding the phrase "because there is no sublation": the meaning is also because of the force of the explanation provided by the scripture itself through its mention in another place.

Nor is the meaning merely that [the world] is illusion alone. Now, one might ask: "In the absence of the word *nāmadheya* (name), how is it established that the manifold of names (*nāma-prapañca*) is merely an object of speech? To this he says: "Of the name also... [The phrase] "established by scripture" means it is established by the previously cited scripture: "Thou art that. Now, one might object: "In the case of the view that 'thou art not that' (*atattvamasi*), the form should have been 'thou shalt be' (*āso'si*). He raises this doubt with the word "might be" (*bhavet*). [This applies] even in the absence of such a sentence.

The meaning is: even in the absence of specific statements characterized by indicators such as restatement (*anuvāda*) and so forth, or words such as *tat* (that) and the like, and the application of logical reasoning (*yukti*). "The Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is spoken of" means the pure Brahman (*śuddhabrahman*). "Otherwise" means if the world were grasped in the Supreme Self by means of scripture (*śruti*). Having accepted that the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) refers exclusively to the qualified Brahman (*viśiṣṭabrahman*), he states the meaning: "Of the Lord alone. The word should be split as "because of non-establishment" (*asiddheḥ*). "By that" means by perception (*pratyakṣa*). "In the third [alternative]" means...

The meaning is: "the position that [the scripture] teaches the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Previously, this was interpreted as a response to an objection; now, with reference to the argument regarding the futility of the scripture (*śrutivaiyyarthya*), he interprets it as being intended to state another argument, beginning with the words "for this reason also" (*itaśca*). The word "stated" (*uktā*) means the defect consisting of futility. The phrase "caused by that" (*tannimitta*) means caused by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). He explains the root text, "the limiting adjunct," by breaking it down into parts through supplementary statements, from the words "only produced by the limiting adjunct" (*upādhikṛta eva*) up to "the state of being" (*bhāvaḥ*).

"And for the purpose of refuting" means that another fault [is to be stated]; this refers to what will be said later, such as in the eleventh [chapter]. He states the meaning of the word *hantṛ* (killer) as "the agent of separation from the body," and the meaning of the word *hata* (slain) as "separated from the body. [The word] "by me" [is used].

The meaning is that there is a contradiction with the eleven statements [of the Lord], such as: "Slay those who have already been slain by me; stand firm and fight; you shall be the victor in battle over your enemies. The phrase "this very verse" is used because the commentary has interpreted it in that manner—this is the intended sense. "By this" means by the explanation that "the Supreme Person does not [slay]. The sense is that in this view, there is no other person [who slays]. "The reason has been stated" means that regarding the statement "He does not slay independently," the reason consisting of his lack of independence has been stated. "Absence of such conceit" [is the meaning].

The meaning is that the absence of the conceit of independence (*svātantryābhimāna*) regarding being the killer or the killed, etc., is stated there as the cause for the lack of knowledge regarding the agency of killing and so forth by way of independence. If a knower (*jñānī*) kills an enemy or is killed, then that knower does not know his own independence in being killed; this is because of the absence of the conceit consisting of the delusion of independence, or else because of the absence of the conceit [of identity] with the body and so forth—this is the intended sense. "Because it was stated immediately before" means by the word *purāṇa* (ancient); this is the thought. He connects the root text.

"Regarding the union with and separation from the body": this means for the purpose of removing this doubt. Even though there is no destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*) over time or due to causes such as the destruction of its reflection (*bimba*), there might still be destruction through specific causes such as weapons encountered in battle; it is for the removal of this doubt that [the text says] so. "Because it was stated immediately before": this means because it was stated in the first half-verse. To the question, "How is the Gītā passage to be construed with the half-verse 'eternal, omnipresent, and atomic'?", he says: "Eternal... [and so on].

Alternatively, he states the meaning of the root verse, "the all-pervading, immovable pillar" (*sarvagatasthāṇu*), by connecting it with the word "eternal" (*nitya*). The sense is that otherwise, a discrepancy would arise between the commentary and the text being commented upon. Thus, "the cause of dissimilarity has been shown" means that although the individual soul (*jīva*) shares with the Lord (*īśvara*) such qualities as being indivisible, there is no total identity; here, the reasons consisting of "all-pervasiveness" and "atomicity" have been shown. Furthermore, it is appropriate that "immovable" (*acala*), which denotes the absence of action, serves as a qualification of the all-pervasive one.

"Because motion is not observed in space and other all-pervading things; therefore, the word 'all-pervading' (*sarvagata*) must be understood as a separate term"—this is the objection raised with the words "here," etc. To explain the phrase "for this very reason," it is said: "because of the presentation of a reason. This means: because of the presentation of a reason—namely, being bound by injunctions and prohibitions—in support of the probandum, which is the lack of independence (*asvātantrya*) expressed by the term "residing in the all-pervading" (*sarvagatastha*). "In this position" means: in the position that the first half-verse refers to Īśvara. "By the reason of eternality (*sanātanatva*), etc. [is the meaning].

The meaning is: "by reason of the soul's being bound by injunctions and prohibitions and its being a reflection. He states the object of the reference "therefore" (tasmāt) with the words beginning "since" (yasmāt). He states the full sense of "therefore" (tasmāt) with the words beginning "therefore, from battle and so forth" (tasmād yuddhādīti). He states the attainment of the word "their" (teṣām) with the word "me" (mām).
"But those who, having renounced all actions in Me and being devoted to Me,
worship Me while meditating on Me with an exclusive yoga alone."

The meaning is that because it is heard [mentioned] in the first half [of the scripture], it refers to the twelfth chapter. The word *atha* (now/then) is used here in the sense of introducing a new topic (*arthāntara*). "One" (*eka*) refers to the form of the Lord (*bhagavadrūpa*). The meaning is that He was introduced as an illustration for the beginningless and eternal nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Regarding the phrase "not there, nor there" (*na ca tatra tatra*): the commentary (*bhāṣya*) has stated that the passage "But the indestructible" (*avināśi tu*) refers to the Vedas and so forth; whereas the passage "of the undecaying" (*anāśinaḥ*) refers to the individual soul, and the passage "the indestructible" (*avināśinam*) refers to the individual soul by means of the explanation "devoid of connection with the body," and so on. Therefore, the meaning is that there would be a contradiction [with that commentary].

Regarding the phrase "the suspicion of tautology and so forth": in the Bhāṣya, the uprooting of the two suspicions—of tautology and of futility—was accomplished by the argument that even when identity is stated, there is no tautology regarding the oneness of the Lord because specific qualifications not previously mentioned are being introduced. Here, however, since the explanation follows the primary sense of the words, such a suspicion does not even arise; thus, the intention is that no further uprooting of those suspicions is required. Regarding the phrase "of the subverting arguments": the meaning is that this has already been stated in passages such as, "Nor is there fullness of the individual souls (jīvas) in terms of space or qualities, for nothing is pervaded by the jīva," and so forth.

"Of another matter" means of that which consists of the Vedas and so forth. "Because the connection has been stated" means because it has been introduced at the beginning of every verse as being logically connected; this is the sense. "As a supplement to this" means because of the explanation of the phrase "not from the non-existent" (*nāsataḥ*) as "happiness and suffering do not arise from good and evil deeds," and because it was stated here that "worship of Him is indeed a good deed," and thus it was said, "therefore, fight for His sake"; this is the sense. "In the manner already stated."

Furthermore, it is established that for living beings, perfection in terms of place and quality does not exist, and that suffering is incurred through the loss of the body and so forth even against one's will. Therefore, "fight for the sake of honoring the imperishable object of knowledge"—this is the meaning according to the direction previously stated. Regarding the phrase "of this": the word "declares its utility" is to be supplied by ellipsis. He clarifies the reason stated as "for this very reason" with the words beginning "this [self] is not... and so on. [The term] "in the present context" refers to...

The meaning is that [the verse] "But indeed not... is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the eternality of the living self (*jīva*) introduced in the preceding verse, as well as the mere acquisition of a natural body introduced by the words "in this body" (*asmin dehe*), because of the subsequent mention of "by means of the body" (*śarīreṇa*) and "is eternal" (*nityaḥ*). "For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means "precisely because of the restatement. "Because it has been stated" (*uktatvāt*) means "because it has been stated in the passage beginning with 'They have an end' (*antavantaḥ*)," etc.; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the term "eternality" (*nityatva*) is included. This is how the connection (*anvaya*) of the phrase "this [verse] has proceeded" (*ity etat pravṛttam*) is to be understood. "Because of the mention of an additional qualification" (*adhika-viśeṣaṇa-ukteḥ*)...

The intention is that the matter is fully established by the statements "He is neither born nor dies" and "Unborn, eternal. [Regarding the phrase] "the meaning has already been explained": this should be understood as being by means of the statement "He is not slain. The intention is that the explanation is given thus: "While the body is being slain by the independent Lord, He is not slain. [Regarding the phrase] "by way of the sequence of descents": because of His indestructibility, beginninglessness, eternity, and so forth, there is the descent of His independence; by that, there is the descent of His status as the creator of all; and by that, [the answer to] "whom does He cause to be slain?"—this is the meaning of "by way of the sequence of descents."

He clarifies what was stated by the phrase "by this" with the words beginning "how," etc. Regarding the phrase "because of being thus dependent": the meaning is that the root of these [arguments] is "because of hearing" (from scripture); by the word "etc.," the inclusion of "being the creator of all" is intended. Regarding the phrase "because of the statement of its existence": the meaning is that in the ninth chapter of the first book (*Skandha*), within the *Bhīṣmastuti*, there is a statement regarding states such as being cut, etc. Regarding the phrase "the refutation of the cutting of the body, etc.": the intention is that this refers to the verse beginning with "not him" (*nainam*). Regarding the phrase "also for each qualifier": [this is the sense].

The meaning is that the phrase "this one" (*enam*), which serves as a specific qualification such as "does not cut" and "does not burn"—indicating the absence of cutting, burning, and so forth—suggests a construction through repetition (*vīpsā*), namely by connecting it with many instances of the word "this" (*enam enam*) and likewise by connecting it with many instances of the word "this" (*ayam ayam*). He states the meaning of two words from the remainder of the Śruti passage: "He whose light is knowledge, whose supreme effort is true, who knows all knowledge, who is bliss among blisses, Viṣṇu, the supreme imperishable. This refers to the beginning of the passage starting with "who knows all knowledge" (*jñānajñāna*). [This is indicated by] the word "Śruti."

The meaning is: "precisely because of the injunctions of such scriptural passages as 'formless and imperishable' and 'the bodiless self consisting of consciousness,' and so forth. He says "na ca" (not) to mark the conclusion of the sentence, since it begins as a separate section; thus, the connection is with the word "asti" (it exists).

Immediately after the word "viśeṣa" (particularity), he provides the construction by supplying the words "exists" (*asti*) and so forth, beginning with the phrase "by [the words] 'exists,' etc. Regarding the term "qualified" (*viśeṣita*), the meaning is "possessing a particularity" (*viśeṣavat*). Regarding the phrase "by a succession of differences" (*bhedaparamparayā*): the difference between the particularity and the qualified object is distinct from its own substrates, namely the particularity and the qualified object; that difference, in turn, is distinct from the two things that serve as its own substrates. Such is the meaning of "by a succession of differences. In this context, the word "therein" (*tatra*) is a restatement, while "Lord" (*īśvara*) is the explanation. He states this to avoid redundancy with the word "only" (*eva*).

"Experiencing the notion of oneness and 'I'" means "nothing as manifold. "These are the scriptural texts" means the scriptural texts beginning with "only one," and so forth. The word division is "of non-difference and of distinction. "'Distinction, the qualified, and so forth' means in the conventional usage such as 'this is the distinction' and 'this is the qualified,' etc. "O Lakṣmaṇa," and so forth.

The meaning is that in the Rāma incarnation, Śeṣa, Sanatkumāra, and Aniruddha were born as Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna; and in the Kṛṣṇa incarnation, they were born as Bala, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, while Śeṣa was born as Nara, and Indra and the others were born as Arjuna and so forth. Regarding the word "himself" (svayam): it means that Kṛṣṇa stated such arguments as that because the soul is eternal, the destruction of the body is unavoidable, and therefore the resolution of the decay and fall [of the body] is achieved through obtaining a suitable [new] one.

Now, explaining the reason why it was stated in the verse beginning with "atha cet" that sorrow should not be felt, he states the meaning of the root text: "The rule of birth and death applies here. This means in the verse beginning with "atha cet. Alternatively, "here" means in the verse beginning with "atha cet," as well as in the two subsequent verses intended to explain it. "'Previously'" means in passages such as "eternal, omnipresent, immovable. Thus it has been said.

The meaning of the verse beginning with "nainam" is that the Lord possesses sovereignty because there is no cutting or other such destruction even of His body. The phrase "in some cases" implies that the notion of [the Lord's] sovereignty must be cultivated. The phrase "as stated" means it is in the form of a summary of the sovereignty established in the section on the Lord (*īśvara*). The intention is that there is no tautology with the passage beginning with "nainam. The phrase "because of the perception" refers to the suffix *-vat* (denoting likeness). The phrase "a collection of oceans" [is explained as follows].

The intention is that the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhāccha* was not adopted; rather, only the suffix *aṇ* was adopted. Consequently, regarding the phrase "from that" (*tataḥ*), having accepted that it means "from that cause" or "from Hari," he says: "dependent on that" (*tadadhīna*). Regarding the phrase "of what was said" (*ityuktasya*), the meaning is: "of the doubt concerning victory expressed by Arjuna. With the intention of applying the rule *ājjaserasuk*, he says: "the heroes" (*śūrāḥ*). [These are] those who abandon their bodies in principal battles.

He states the meaning of the remainder of the Śruti passage, "May he also go to that which belongs to those who give a thousand-fold sacrificial fee," beginning with the words "And those who... and so forth. The sense is that this is because of the scriptural hearing: "May he go to those who fight. This has already been stated.

Having concluded with the first quarter-verse (*pāda*)—“But these are not [the Self]” (*na tv ime*) and so forth—that which was stated regarding the essential nature of the reality of the living soul (*jīva-tattva*), a different method for describing the means of knowledge (*jñānopāya*) is now commenced; that is to say, a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) is made in the second quarter-verse. To the question, “What is the distinction between these two, since both are censured? he says: “Of these two mentioned here. “But not in this world” (*na tv aihike*): the meaning is that they are not accepted as being causes for results pertaining to this life (*aihika*). “But here again” (*atra punar*)... [etc.]

The analysis of the words is *rājyārtham* (for the sake of the kingdom). Regarding the phrase *sopapattikam*: the meaning is that it possesses another attribute (*dharmāntara*), namely the quality of establishing the subject matter explained in the preceding and subsequent sections, accompanied by the logical justification (*upapatti*) characterized by the absence of contradiction. By this, the intended sense is that the very means of knowledge (*jñānopāya*) are the meanings of the terms *Sāṅkhya* and *Yoga*, and not anything else, because there would otherwise be a contradiction with what was stated previously and subsequently. He states the meaning of the term *niṣiddhaparityāga* (renunciation of the prohibited): "having another object. The meaning is that it is not practiced as having another deity as its object.

"Endowed with that" means endowed with the dharma of the three Vedas. "Established by implication" means that since it has been stated that [the limit] is merely reaching heaven and not the attainment of eternal hell, it follows by implication that one attains liberation in due course; this is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Liberation belongs to this very person" implies that liberation belongs to the devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata) alone, so why is it said that for the knower of the three Vedas (traividya), the limit is merely reaching heaven?

Alternatively, the meaning is: "What is expressed by the statement, 'He is called a speaker of the Veda' (*vedavādī sa ucyate*), regarding this very person who acts contrary to the essential points taught in the three Vedas? Immediately after the word *abhipretam* (intended), one should supply the phrase: "by which [reason] the status of being a speaker of the Veda would result for both the Bhāgavata and the Traividya. To avoid redundancy, he states the difference in meaning with the words beginning *anārambham*. Regarding the phrase *kāraṇaparityāgena*: the meaning is "by abandoning that which is the cause of the intellect characterized by lack of resolve. Immediately after the word *tathā*, he states the remainder [of the sentence].

"Taking as its object" (*viṣayīkārī*): To the question "Of what word does 'end' (*anta*) mean the meaning?", he says: "'End' means... "Regarding the stated meaning": the meaning is that this [action] is prohibited by the words "this which" (*yām imām*) and so forth, because it is contrary to the previously stated practice of performing action without desire through the intellect of offering to the Blessed One. "This earth" means either this inferior ground or hell. "'As it has been said'": the meaning is that it has been stated that this is the object of others. "The natural [state] is enjoined": this should be connected with the phrase "and that is improper, therefore he says."

However, if the reading is *kiṃ vidhīyate*, then it is exactly as heard [in the text]. "Of this" (*asya*) means "of its being under the control of that. "The contradiction with 'practice yoga' and so forth" means the contradiction with the words from the *Gītā* stated in the fourth chapter. Regarding "not included," it should be construed with the phrase "and not liberated. It is said to be "inferior" because of the mention of "the other" (*para*). The meaning of "all this" (*sarvam idam*) is expressed by changing the word order as "in all this. "Without a sign" (*apraketa*) means "unrecognized."

The meaning of *āḥ* is "it was. The meaning of *idam agre* is "in the beginning of this"; that is, at the beginning of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). The meaning of *āpaḥ* is "devoid of a protector. The plural number is due to the inherent nature of the word. The lengthening of the vowel *a* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), or it may be derived from the prefix *āṅ*. He states the meaning in accordance with the context as "surpassing all. This means "surpassing everything in comparison. With the intention that the word *te* (they) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), he says: "all living beings."

"Because there is no proposition (*pratijñā*). This means that there is no proposition stating that "the cultivation of unity (*aikyabhāvanā*) should not be performed. The intention is that this follows from the reasoning regarding its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). To obtain the proposition that [the world] is neither existent nor non-existent, he says: "The meaning is 'by the mind'. Regarding the phrase "it has been stated," it should be connected with the first half of the verse beginning with "from afar" (*dūreṇa*). "As before" means that it should be connected with "they think by the mind" (*manasā manyante*), just as in the passage "Do not be motivated by the fruit of action" (*mā karmaphalahetur bhūḥ*).

The sense is that by this, the attainment of the meaning "those who cultivate the realization of oneness" is obtained. Alternatively, one might ask: how is the cultivation of oneness obtained through the term *phalahetu* (cause of the fruit)? To address why this [term] is explained in this way, he says: "As before. This means "like [the passage] beginning with *mā karmaphalahetur bhūḥ*. *Phalahetu* refers to the Lord (*īśvara*). The meaning is: "those who, in their minds, become causes of the fruit"; that is, those who think, "I am the Lord, the cause of the fruit," as in the previous case. The meaning is that such persons are not objects of compassion.
Alternatively, the meaning is that the objects of compassion are themselves pitiable. This is introduced in the commentary on the verse beginning with "one who is endowed with wisdom" (buddhiyukta).

He introduces the second half of the verse with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Regarding "But surely" (*nanu*): the meaning of "apply yourself to yoga" (*yogāya yujyasva*) is that knowledge is to be attained. In the phrase "due to the absence [of knowledge] and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the knowledge of the Lord and other such qualities. Regarding "in this [verse]": the meaning is that since only renunciation (*tyāga*) and equanimity (*samatva*) are stated to be the meaning of the word "yoga" in the verse, the knowledge of the Lord is not included as the meaning of the word "yoga. Regarding "here too": the meaning is "even in the verse beginning 'one whose intellect is disciplined' (*buddhiyukta*). Regarding "immediate" (*aparokṣa*): the meaning is the immediate [knowledge] denoted by the word "wise one" (*manīṣi*).

"In the previous [verse]" means that, following an exposition of the meaning of this verse, the fruit of knowledge mentioned in the term "crossing over the delusion of the intellect" is now stated. "In the [verse] beginning with 'śruti'" means that it is also so in the verse beginning with "yogasthaḥ. "The connection here also is 'when... then'" means that even in the *Smṛti* [text], the path of the *Śruti* is intended. Since the repetition of the word "tuṣṭa" (satisfied) in the root text would otherwise be purposeless, he states its function with the words "How could there not be the transcendence of the individual soul, etc. and so forth. And [the phrase] "in the thorough knowledge of the cause and the fruit."

Furthermore, when one fully understands through tradition that hell and other states result in undesirable consequences, a realization arises—driven by fear—that attachment and the like are the causes of those states. The abandonment of those [defilements] occurs through the sequential abandonment of their causes, such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). And that abandonment occurs only when there is knowledge of them; therefore, the meaning is that [the Blessed One] spoke of both the cause and the fruit of attachment and so forth. "It has been determined" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while "only," etc., is the explanation (*vyākhyā*). "As previously defined" refers to the definition stated earlier.

The meaning is that what was stated diffusely across the four verses beginning with "he abandons" (*prajahāti*) is now being stated in a condensed form. "Because of the contradiction with the statement" means because of the contradiction with the previously cited statement that "the cessation of all desires does not occur through knowledge in any way whatsoever. "As stated" means the definition of the knower (*jñānin*) as stated in the passage beginning with "he abandons. "By reason of its being difficult to accomplish" means by reason of its being achieved only with great effort; for the suffix *khal* is prescribed after the particles *īṣat*, *dur*, and *su* when they signify difficulty or ease.

"And in the absence of that" means "and in the absence of remembrance. "The effected Brahman" (kāryabrahman) is said for the purpose of excluding Viriñca (Brahmā). The point is that even he is denoted by the neuter term "Brahman" in such passages as "He leads them to Brahman," according to the direction of the Sūtra, "The effected [Brahman], Bādari [says]" (BS 4.3.7); furthermore, the attainment of the Supreme Brahman alone constitutes liberation.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the third chapter.

Hari Om. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is with the phrase "it has been described" (*nirūpitam*), ending with the word "iti. It should also be understood as being connected with the passage beginning with "But never indeed do I... (*na tvevāham...*). With the intention that the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), he says: "It is known" (*jñāyate*). By the word "Īśvara etc. (*īśvarādi*), there is the inclusion of the Lord (*īśvara*) and so forth; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the primary subject under discussion, as well as the Vedas, place, time, and so on, which are mentioned incidentally (*prāsaṃgika*).

Even for those who, because the Lord is engaged in battle, harbor doubts regarding His impermanence, He is addressed as the primary subject through such passages as "But never am I... (*na tv evāham...*) and so forth. Then, following the promise "Hear this [teaching] concerning Yoga" (*yoge tv imāṃ śṛṇu*), the means for the knowledge of the Lord Himself is taught through the passage beginning with "The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their domain" (*traiguṇyaviṣayā vedāḥ*). Therefore, He is referred to by His own name as "the Lord" (*īśvarāt*). For this very reason, it was stated that the means for knowing His essential nature has been explained. [This refers to the phrase] "through the yoga of action and meditation" (*karmadhyānayoga*).

The meaning is that [the distinction] is due to the difference between the means consisting of action and knowledge (*karmarūpa-jñānopāya*) and the means consisting of meditation and knowledge (*dhyānarūpa-jñānopāya*). He states the basis for the prohibition beginning with "not without both" as follows: "By knowledge, according to the Sāṅkhyas. This refers to scriptural passages such as "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 7.1.3) and "We have drunk the Soma, we have become immortal" (*Ṛgveda*), as well as to Smṛti passages such as "by the yoga of knowledge, according to the Sāṅkhyas" (*Bhagavad Gītā* 3.3). Regarding the phrase "for not": the sense is that the mere absence of action is impossible. Regarding the phrase "not complete": the meaning is that in liberation, there is the experience of all the bliss appropriate to one's own capacity.

The sense is that [liberation] is to be accomplished by knowledge assisted by subsequent action. He offers another interpretation of that very same statement: "Then let it be so. By this—meaning by the statement beginning with "nor without knowledge"—the deluded person objects: "In this world, in *saṃsāra*, there is a firm standing (*niṣṭhā*) through knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas and through action for the Yogins, but not liberation. He addresses this with the words beginning "It might be so here," and so on, [concluding with] "And that is not the case here."

The meaning is that the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is the cause for [the existence of] the collection. "Codya" (to be questioned) means "having raised the objection" by means of the words beginning with "bhavet" (it might be). "Svānadhīnam" means not dependent on the individual soul (*jīva*). "Jñānarūpatvāt" means because its very nature is the knowledge of all things; for the suffix *ka* is prescribed only in the sense of an agent according to the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. "Hetvantaram" (another reason) means...

The meaning is that the reason stated in the form of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) in the four verses beginning with "Those who perform sacrifice with sacrifice" (*sahayajñāḥ*) is another reason consisting in being the one who sets the wheel in motion. And regarding the phrase "and the postulation of another meaning": this means the postulation that the words *brahman* and *akṣara* signify the Veda and the Supreme Brahman, respectively. He shows the etymological derivation of the word *yoga* as stated in the Smṛti: "Supreme" (*param*), meaning "highest. The elision of the final syllable of the word *para* is due to its being explained [in the Nirukta]; this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "by another reason": [it refers to the reason previously mentioned].

The meaning is: "by means of another reason consisting in the contradiction with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), rather than by considering the contradiction with the *Smṛti* in the form of its commentary. Regarding "because it is useless": the intention is that, however, in our own position (*svapakṣa*), utility has already been stated. Regarding "due to the absence of origination": the intention is that the Veda is eternal. Regarding "from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*): one would have to say that the syllable (*akṣara*) arises from the elements for the sake of establishing the [Vedic] wheel; for Brahman, denoted by the word "syllable," is not produced by the elements—this is the meaning. Regarding "the postulation of a different meaning": [this refers to the opponent's attempt to avoid the contradiction].

The meaning is that the conceptualization is as follows: from the Veda, which consists of the words of the Supreme Lord, proceeds the engagement of persons in action; from that, the accomplishment of action; from that, rain; from that, food; from that, the elements; and from the elements, the engagement in action. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the Supreme Brahman is included. Now, one might object: let it simply be "the imperishable source of beings" (bhūta-sambhava); let the word *sambhava* be taken to mean manifestation (*vyakti*). To this he says: "for the sake of manifestation" and "because of the difference in meaning."

The meaning is that there is a difference in purpose, consisting of the joy of having accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatva*). He says, "By action alone [is liberation]," etc., with the intention of explaining the meaning as "performing only action. Regarding the phrase "because it has been stated," the sense is that this has been stated either in the passage beginning with "Together with sacrifice" (*saha-yajñā*) or in the passage beginning with "Not by the yoga of action for the yogins" (*na karma-yogena yoginām*). To ensure consistency between the first and second halves of the verse, he says, "the word 'of them' (*teṣām*) should be supplied. "Another reason is being stated" means that, in view of proper conduct, another reason—namely, the winning over of the world (*loka-saṃgraha*)—is being stated.

The two instances of "of this" (*ityasya*) are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). It should be understood that the specific distinction regarding being preceded by attachment or non-attachment has already been stated in the verse beginning with "those who are attached" (*saktāḥ*). Having taken the meaning of "having renounced" (*saṃnyasya*) to be "having abandoned," he says: "It is contradictory. [He explains] "the state of being free from possessiveness" (*nirmamatvam*); the meaning is that the state of being free from possessiveness is explained by the phrase "I am not the doer. After the words "worship performed by me," he states the remainder.

The determination [of the text] beginning with "tat-pūjā" (worship of That) is appropriate. The meaning is that by the phrase "devotion to That" (tad-bhakti), the state of being free from desire (niraśitva) is explained. He states a qualification for the term "renunciation of action" (karmanyāsa): "endowed with freedom from possessiveness and freedom from desire. Regarding the phrase "by such division" (ityādi vibhāgena): where the agency belongs to the individual soul (jīva) alone, there the agency is dependent on another; where the agency belongs to primordial nature (prakṛti) alone—as in passages such as "for one is made to perform action helplessly by all the qualities born of nature"—there the agency is of the nature of a modification (vikāra); this is what should be understood. Regarding the phrase "it does not exist" and so forth, [the meaning is] by such division.

The meaning is that where the soul's lack of agency is stated—in passages such as "the soul is not the agent, nor are the actions [its own]"—therein there is no independent agency belonging to itself; whereas where it is stated that "nature is not the agent," there it should be understood in the sense that there is no agency preceded by knowledge and desire. After the Smṛti passage beginning with "from its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*), which serves to explain the phrase "of nature" (*prakṛteḥ*) and so forth, the Smṛti passage beginning with "because" (*yasmāt*) should be recited. He says this because it must follow the Gītā verse that is to be explained.

By the words "mayītyādītyādinā" (by the phrase beginning with "in me," etc.), [the author] indicates the utility [of the introduction]. The sense is that this is because the threefold agency mentioned in the *Smṛti* is intended [to apply] to *prakṛti* in the statement [beginning with] "because... He clarifies the utility for the explanation by saying "in the passage beginning with 'prakṛteḥ' (of *prakṛti*)," which is to be connected with the second half-verse beginning with "ahaṅkāra" (ego). The syntactical connection of the word "ityādi" (etc. is with the phrase "the preparation of the foundation. The meaning is: for the purpose of providing a direct explanation of verses such as "for one is made to act helplessly by karma. [This refers to] the *Jayā* and other [commentaries].

The meaning is that we observe a transformation into other forms, such as Hiraṇyākṣa and Rāvaṇa, among those like Jaya and Vijaya. "Mixed" means that the qualities consist of both innate knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). "And so forth should be applied" means that one should apply the principle that knowledge of reality is innate and devotion (*bhakti*) is innate. "And therefore" means because the qualities such as false knowledge are innate. "What follows from this? means what is the consequence of this?

"Thus, etc. means that He causes those who possess middling qualities to perform both good and bad actions, while He causes those who possess inferior qualities to perform only bad actions. "By Viṣṇu" is a restatement (anuvāda); "of Viṣṇu," etc., is the explanation. "Deluded by them" means deluded by the mixed qualities. Regarding the term "non-existence" (abhāva), it should be construed with "knowledge and so forth. He states the meaning through a change of expression: "dependent on Viṣṇu. Regarding "by nature": the meaning is the cessation of activity that follows one's own inherent nature.

He shows the relevance of raising the question with the words "of those two," etc. The phrase "because it has already been stated" means that the intention is that even Hari is denoted by the word *prakṛti* because of the reason [given] that he possesses preeminent agency (*prakṛṣṭakṛtimattva*). To refute the objection that this is merely a question about something already established, he says: "the remainder is thus. The meaning of "this is not so" is that the question regarding a powerful impeller is directed only toward those who impel through base desires and the like, but not toward the Lord or the gods who impel both the superior and the inferior. [The phrase] "even in the case of the stated meaning" refers to the same point.

The word "also" (*api*) [in the phrase] "even in the sense already stated, such as 'from the Supreme Lord, from Āditya,' etc. is used to include that sense. The word "also" is used to include the collective explanation of the verses. Regarding the phrase "of this [verse] beginning with 'kāma'": the meaning is "of the verse containing the refutation. Regarding the phrase "etc.": the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) is that one should understand that, just as rust or impurity (*kalmaṣa*) excessively covers a mirror, so too does [ignorance] excessively cover the lowest person, just as the outer membrane (*ulba*) covers the embryo. Regarding the phrase "of the [verse] beginning with 'indriyāṇi,' etc.": the meaning is "of the two verses beginning with that. He states the meaning of the word "etc.":

"Thus [it is] with Sarasvatī. Regarding "the conceit of possessing discernment": the meaning of "not the other" is "not by way of conceiving oneself as superior," and so forth. He states the meaning of the portion "this is what is meant" as "this word 'is'. For the word "that," the corresponding term is "therein. Its meaning is "in the objection beginning with 'āpaḥ'."

In the *Aitareya* [Āraṇyaka], in the section beginning with "Āpaḥ, Āpaḥ," when the objection was raised as to how the goddess Ramādevī could have the name "Āpaḥ" (Waters) among the gods, the resolution stated by this sentence is that since the gods are the sons of the Blessed One, and since the father, the Blessed One, is designated by the name "Āpaḥ," the sons likewise bear that same name; such is the meaning.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad-Gītā-tātparya-ṭīkā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. "Because it has been explained" means that since the non-performance of action was censured in passages such as "Not by the non-commencement of actions," and so forth, while its performance was enjoined in passages such as "Perform obligatory action," and so forth, [the doctrine] has already been explained. Having grasped the summary of the meaning, he objects: "If this is a summary of the Pañcarātra... [He replies: "The aforementioned inconsistency remains."

The meaning is that there would be an inconsistency regarding Arjuna—described here as a direct incarnation of Indra, a person of the highest qualification, and the dearest to the Lord—as well as regarding his state of being a knower (jñānitva), which was described as "the knowledge of the Pārthas has attained firm stability," were he not to be protected. The word *bhavataḥ* ends in the genitive case; its meaning is "of you. This is because the contradiction with the Śrutis and other authorities has already been stated. Regarding the second [alternative], the meaning is that this has already been stated during the explanation of the phrase "these [bodies] have an end" (*antavanta ime*).

Alternatively, the intention is that this is because [the word *ayam*] is used as an example in passages such as "with body" (*sadeha*) during the explanation of the verse beginning with "they do not cut him" (*na enaṃ chindanti*). Having accepted the meaning that "this activity, consisting of the will for creation and so forth, is the very nature of the Lord," he states the meaning of the word *ayam*: "And this nature is the Lord himself," etc. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of something else": the meaning is "in the sense of being merely the well-known primordial matter (*prakṛti*). The word division is *na aniṣṭam*. He explains the addition of the final word preceded by the restatement of the phrase "by means of surrendering to me."

"By surrendering to Me, [the end is attained]"—this is the implied remainder. Regarding the statement "but the rajasic men there, O Brahmins," he says this in accordance with the purport of the final half-verse: "among those who are rajasic-sattvic. It does not mean merely the definition of a caste; rather, it should be understood that being *sāttvika* is the characteristic of a Vaiṣṇava, while being *tāmasa* is the characteristic of one who hates the Lord. Regarding the term "natural" (*svābhāvika*), the meaning is: one who is a Brāhmaṇa and so forth by his very nature, and not merely by birth. Regarding the term "well-known" (*prasiddha*).

The meaning is that [the state] consists either in the cessation of all activity or in exclusive devotion to the Blessed Lord alone. If one asks, "In that case, what is it?", he says: "Rather, it is devotion to Viṣṇu. Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": the meaning is [the state] of agency and non-agency residing in different substrates. Since the doubt regarding non-difference would not arise if "me" were not mentioned, yet if it were mentioned, how could that doubt be dispelled—he clarifies both points with the words beginning "of himself," and so forth.

One might object: "According to the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṣaḥ samānapade*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs only within a single word (*samānapade*) when it follows the letters *r* or *ṣ*. Since the words *karman* and *naśana* do not reside in a single word here, how can there be the substitution of *ṇ*? To this, he says: "Of that which does not reside in a single word. The meaning is: just as the substitution of *ṇ* is observed for the *n* following the word *brahman* in the phrase *he indra no brahma upayāhi*, so it is here as well. This *ṇ*-substitution is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

The meaning of "of this and so forth" (*ityādeḥ*) is as follows: [the word *bhāva*] also occurs from the beginning of the second quarter [of the verse] in such forms as "from me, who am devoid of action" (*vikarmaṇo naḥ mattaḥ bhavati*). Regarding the phrase "ending in the letter *s*" (*sakārānta iti*): it is because [the word *kara*] is explained in the *Nirukta* in the sense that "in this living being (*jīve*), the rule of action (*karmavidhiḥ*) is measured (*mīyate*), i.e., made an object," which implies a secondary derivative suffix (*upapada-ṭilopa*) after the root *māṅ* (to measure) with the suffix *kanin*. The meaning of "by this" (*anena*) is: by stating that the word *kara* denotes the "rule of action" (*karmavidhi*). [Thus it is said: "the hand (*kara*) is measured."
