The meaning is that the "rule of action" (karmavidhi) is measured, i.e., known. He states the introduction to the verse according to the direction given in the Bhāṣya: "Not only... [referring to] "of both the ignorant and the wise," etc. This refers to the second chapter of the *Tātparya* [on the *Brahmasūtra*], in passages such as "Hari is the refuge of both the ignorant and the wise, and of those who are liberated. Regarding the phrase "of that object": the meaning is "of the object which is the focus of the conceit of independence. Regarding "without determining": the meaning is "without making known," and also "without having understood."

"It is explained as that" means the performance of homas and so forth in the form described for the sake of sacrifice. "Connected with what precedes" means having attained a connection with what precedes in the form of the detailed exposition (*prapañca*). "By way of being connected with what precedes" means by way of being intent upon stating the varieties of sacrifice; or else, it means by way of being connected with the preceding verse beginning with *brahmārpaṇam*. The same applies further on. With the intention that the locative case in the word "dhanuṣi" is a locative of reference (*viṣaya-saptamī*) and serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the knowledge [of the Self], he says: "as the object of the knowledge of the bow."

"The meaning is indeed well-known" means it is of the form "there is no ritual action after [the realization of] knowledge. "Having said" means having said by the verse beginning with "Superior is the sacrifice consisting of the Self to that which consists of material objects. He speaks out of the delusion that the word *atho* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "If it were so" refers to the equality of possessing that [nature], meaning because of the similarity in possessing the nature of the Supreme Self; the intention is that Hari is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the fifth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. "Combined" (samuccita) means that Karma-yoga, which possesses two parts, was promised in the words "I shall declare that action to you," and was then defined by the passage beginning with "For even from action... (Gītā 3.4). Regarding "Yoga": the performance of action with the intention of offering it to the Lord is Yoga; the renunciation of desire is Saṃnyāsa. The phrase "as stated in such passages" refers to the fact that what was taught in the second chapter in the verse beginning "Established in Yoga, perform actions... (Gītā 2.48) is elaborated upon in the third and fourth chapters; thus it is said, "as stated in such passages."

He states the intended meaning of the two halves of the preceding and following *Gītā* verses [XVIII.65–66] with the words "of both" (*ubhayoḥ*). Then, with the words "as to its own nature" (*svarūpe*), he refutes the objection that it is improper to speak of the superiority of one over the other after having stated that both bring about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). The phrase "due to impossibility" (*asambhavāt*) means that performance [of action] with the intention of offering it to the Lord is impossible in the absence of the renunciation of desire and so forth. Here, the word "here" (*atra*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while "having renounced," etc., is the explanation (*vyākhyā*). This is because renunciation has been mentioned separately.

The meaning is that this is because of the statement in the *Aṣṭādaśa* (Mahābhārata): "The wise declare the renunciation of the fruits of all actions to be true renunciation. Regarding the phrase "separate mention," [the author] states the intended meaning of the application of the term "office" (*adhikāra*) in the tenth book (*Daśama-skandha*). He says, "the path of knowledge," and so forth. Here, the word "Smṛti" means: without knowledge there is no perfect performance of action, and without action there is no capacity for knowledge to be a means for attaining its full fruit. This is the sense here.

Alternatively, the meaning is that "in this sense" refers to the fact that knowledge and action possess correctness only through their mutual association. Regarding the phrase "by means of reasoning, etc.": the meaning is that the correctness of knowledge and action, which are to be accomplished by both, is established by reasoning (*yukti*)—specifically, by the impossibility of such correctness otherwise—and by traditional authority (*smṛti*). Regarding the phrase "the explanation of the second half [of the verse]": the meaning is that the first quarter-verse beginning with *mokṣa* explains the term *yoga* (in the expression "the sage joined in yoga"), while the two subsequent quarters beginning with *brahma* provide the explanation of the word *bhadra*.

Regarding "of the first half": the other arrangement [of the words] is clearly explained by the statement "it is auspicious" (*bhadra*). Regarding "that": the meaning is that it is the explanation of the first half. Regarding "it should not be performed": the meaning is that the conjunction is made by way of the intellect (*buddhi*). Regarding "because it will be stated later": this should be connected with the subsequent chapter. Regarding "otherwise": the meaning is the acceptance of the word *ādhāna* as having the sense of non-performance. Regarding "by the phrase 'all rituals'": the meaning is by the third verse that follows. Regarding "by this": [the reference is to the aforementioned].

The phrase "and in the case of action not being perceived" means by way of stating the difference in meaning between the words *kartṛ* (agent) and *arma* (instrument). The term *sarvātmanā* (in its entirety) connects both with what precedes and what follows. Regarding the expression "because it is its own nature," the meaning is: because it does not depend on anything else for its own subsistence or for performing other actions. He states the remainder [of the argument] as: "It would be [the case] for Brahman. The phrase "of the Upaniṣads" means of those beginning with "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite. The word "vyāvṛtteḥ" (exclusion) connects with the word "nibandhanatva" (the state of being the basis).

"Because of the consequence of its exclusion from that" means "because of the consequence of its exclusion from non-existence. "Because impossibility has already been stated" refers to the point made during the explanation of the phrase "and the specific object to be excluded. "By this" means by the commentary beginning with "But non-existence... The meaning is that it is indicated [in the commentary] that Brahman is like a human horn, since its existence is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). "Because it has been refuted" means...

The meaning is that [the view] has been refuted because, without the awakening to qualities such as *sattva*, it is impossible to exclude what is opposed to them, and because it is untenable for Brahman—which is inexpressible—to be the object of a definition (*lakṣya*). He introduces that same statement again by way of another method: "Because of the Lord's lack of agency, etc. The word "because of its being faulty" is to be construed with the phrase "of this opinion. Regarding the phrase "of erroneous knowledge": it means the knowledge of equality toward those who are unequal, such as Brāhmaṇas and others. "Because it has been established" [refers to the aforementioned point].

The phrase "in the second chapter" is to be supplied [to the previous statement]. Regarding the expression "brahmayogādi" (the yoga of Brahman, etc.): the meaning is that it refers to the term *brahmayoga* found in the passage "he whose self is united with the yoga of Brahman. By the word "etc.," passages such as "established in Brahman" and "become Brahman" are included. He states the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) by saying, "it is stated after restating that he is indeed liberated. Thus ends the mention of the ellipsis. Alternatively, the statement of the ellipsis is that immediately after the words "gone to liberation," one says "he is indeed liberated. Because its meaning is difficult to grasp, he clarifies the sense of the pronoun "that" (*tat*) by saying, "because... (referring to the subsequent *yasmāt*).
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the sixth chapter.

Hari Om. "The vow has been made" means that in the second chapter, the discourse on Yoga was vowed. "Karmayoga" means the means to knowledge in the form of action. "In brief" means that it was described briefly in the second chapter with the verse beginning "The objects of the three qualities," and explained in detail in the third chapter and those following. "Up to the end of the fifth" refers to [the instruction] beginning with "having restrained the contacts."

The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādinā*) is to be connected [to the previous context]. "In the midst of *karmayoga*" means "in the midst of the means consisting of action. "Having said this" is to be connected with the preceding half-verse. "Cessation of action" (*karmopaśamaḥ*) means "renunciation of action" (*karmatyāgaḥ*). Having accepted that even one established in *yoga* must perform that [cessation], he raises an objection: "Even by one established in *yoga*. And the phrase "meditation on the Blessed One and so forth" is to be supplied as being expressed by the word "tranquillity" (*śama*). "As previously stated" means "as stated in the passage beginning with 'not without the sacred fires' (*na niragnikaḥ*)," and so on. "Having renounced" (*saṃnyasya*) refers to this [context].

The word "third" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. Regarding the phrase "of one who has ascended to yoga": this means "one whose means [of attainment] are perfected. Since the definition was stated in the verse beginning with "When indeed [the mind is] not in the objects of the senses," he says: "It is explained in detail," using the words beginning with "when," etc.; the word "etc. is used to include several verses. Regarding the phrase "otherwise": the meaning is that if the word *ātman* were to refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the perception of another meaning": the meaning is the perception of the sense of identity (*aikya*). He states the evidence for the fact that the word *ātman* here signifies the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by citing the verse beginning with "the enjoyer," etc. (*bhoktāram iti*).

The meaning is: "in the statement that [the Lord] is to be meditated upon briefly at the end of the fifth [chapter]. "It is established" means: by way of the maxim of *kaimutya* (a fortiori). To ensure that the term "non-devotion" (*ābhakti*) conveys its dependence on persons, he says: "those in whom there is no devotion. "Even there" means: even among those who are devoted. "He worships" (*bhajate*) means: he serves.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Hari Oṃ. "As stated previously" means as stated at the beginning of the first half of the chapter. "For the sake of devotion" implies that devotion consists of affection preceded by the knowledge of [the Lord's] majesty. The analysis of the phrase is "it was not stated. This means it was not stated either here in this chapter or here in the seventh [chapter]. "Desire to obtain" (lipset) means the wish for gain; that is to say, for the purpose of generating reverence. "Thus explained" implies by means of a supplementary statement (śeṣokti). Such is the construction for each term. "By means of the higher, the lower, and so forth," etc.

The meaning is that one must cultivate [the qualities] in a higher, lower, even lower, and even higher degree. He explains this in two ways with the words "because there is nothing else in between" and so forth, starting with "But he is not... and so on. "It has been explained" means it has been explained as being of the nature of consciousness. "Of this" is a restatement of the word "thus. "By the knowledge of the supremacy and so forth of Śrī and the others" is the explanation. "Desires to obtain" (lipset) means with zeal. "Or in the case of gradation" (tāratamye vā) means "or in the case of the gradation previously mentioned," namely, that there would be a gradation.

He states [the meaning] according to the direction given in the Bhāṣya: "that which displays consciousness. He states another meaning for the word *gandhayati*: "and because it bestows a holy fragrance. "Because of its impelling nature" means "because of its impelling nature as a seed. "Another meaning" is to be connected with the word *bala*. "It is a restatement" implies that there is thus no tautology. "In this case too" means "even regarding the meanings of the words *pūrṇarati*, *puṣpa*, and *bala*. "As before" [refers to the previous explanation].

The meaning is as follows: in passages such as "He causes [them] to taste" (*rasayati*), His role as the impeller is as previously stated; likewise, in the phrase "Hari, moreover, does not cause the destruction of dharma," and so forth, since He is the impeller of desires that are not opposed to dharma within the category of "desire" (*kāma*), the construction is to be understood as "desire not opposed to dharma" (*dharmāviruddhakāma*). Regarding the statement "Abiding in water, He causes [it] to taste," etc., he states the supplementary meaning for the sake of the established conclusion of the *Smṛti*: "By the arrangement beginning with 'taste in water'. This means by the following arrangement: "Taste in water, smell in earth, and radiance in the moon and sun," and so on.

He introduces the *Gītā*: "Not merely... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "like the earth and the mountains": the meaning is that the relationship of mutual dependence between the earth and the mountains is likewise [the case here]. Regarding the phrase "in reverse order" (*vailomyena*): the meaning is "by way of prior and posterior. The phrase "because it is an object of knowledge" (*tanmeyatvāt*) is intended to provide the etymological derivation of the word *māyā* with respect to Lakṣmī. He states its meaning: "By Viṣṇu alone... The sense is this: from the root *māṅ* (to measure), with the suffix *ya* in the passive sense, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, [we derive *māyā*]. And [it is said] "by Lakṣmī... and so forth.

The word "ca" (and) has been supplied [in the commentary] for the purpose of conjunction with "jaḍaprakṛtyā" (by the insentient material nature). Regarding the phrase "by this": the meaning is "by the textual passage beginning with 'acetanayā' (by the insentient). It has been stated that by saying "by the material nature" (*prakṛtyā*), either because there is no difference between the material cause and its effect, or because the term serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that which consists of it, the meaning of the passage beginning with "by the three" is thereby explained. Regarding the phrase "of that which removes the doubt": the sense is that the removal of that doubt occurs through the statement that Hari alone is the deluder, having made the two material natures the instrumental cause. Regarding the term "sāmānādhikaraṇyena" (by grammatical coreferentiality): [this refers to the construction of the terms].

The meaning is as follows: if one accepts the analysis of the compound *ekabhakti* as "one whose devotion (*bhakti*) is single," then—given that the feminine form [of a word] becomes masculine when it is a co-referential term following a word that has already been stated in the masculine and does not end in the suffix *-ūṅ*, provided it is not a word for a numeral (ending in *-aṇ-*) or a word in the group beginning with *priya*—the rule prohibits the masculine transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) when words such as *priya* follow. Since the word *bhakti* is included among those beginning with *priya*, the masculine transformation would not apply; thus, even in the compound, the form would result in *ekā bhaktiḥ*. This refers to the aforementioned point.

The meaning is that by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "he attains" (*āpnoti*), the self (*ātman*) is so called; thus, "my self" (*me ātmā*) means "that which possesses my attainment," which is the stated sense. Regarding the word "but" (*tu*): the meaning is "of the word 'but' in the phrase 'the knower, however' (*jñānī tu*). He says "by way of the opposite" because it will be stated later that those who sacrifice with mixed [rites] attain the world of heaven and earth, and thus their attainment of darkness (*tamas*) is not possible [in that context]. "By way of the opposite" means "by way of the opposite of the prescribed rule. He says "having known it erroneously" because the attainment of darkness is not possible through mere ignorance alone. And regarding "another cause": [this refers to...]

It should be understood that, in addition to being born into a family of the ignorant (*ajña-kula*), another cause is the lack of knowledge regarding the Blessed Lord. This is the sense of the phrase "the remainder" (*iti śeṣaḥ*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "one should know that [remainder]. The intention is that by this, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the reality of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇu-tattvaṃ ca*) becomes logically justified. The phrase "knowledge concerning that" (*tad-viṣaya-jñāna*) means knowledge, praise, prostration, and so forth, directed toward other deities. To the question "Why [is it] of that alone? he says: "Of some" (*keṣāṃcit*). And the phrase "this too" (*idaṃ ca*) means the worship of other deities subsequent to the knowledge of the reality of Viṣṇu.

"Among those who possess the threefold knowledge (*traividya*)... means that even for those who know Viṣṇu, there remains the fruit of birth and so forth due to their failure to abandon the worship of other deities. He raises an objection: "By previous [actions]... He replies: "By subsequent... meaning with respect to the worship of other deities occurring after the time of knowing the true nature of Viṣṇu. He raises another objection: "Inherently... [He replies: "Due to a specific cause... meaning consisting of the desire for petty fruits and the like. The phrase "this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇam*)" is to be construed with the words "even in that birth. By this... [the following is established].

The meaning is that by the passage beginning with "and in the case of non-abandonment" (*atyāge ca*), the subject matter (*viṣaya*)—which is inherently of the nature of a pure Bhāgavata—is stated. "Only the aforementioned meaning" means that the word *ātman* has the sense of "attainment" (*prāpti*) alone. "With reference to" (*uddiśya*) implies that the accusative case is used because "going" (*gati*) is the object of reference. The meaning of "the aforementioned self" (*uktātma*) is "of one who worships the Lord. This is the meaning of "resorting to me" (*māmāsthita*). "From the attainment of that" (*tatprāpteḥ*)—this has been applied [to the text].

The meaning is that the statement "Vāsudeva is everything" has been joined with such authoritative means as the proof that He is the complete reality (*pūrṇa-vastu*). The syntactical connection is: "He stated the fruit for that purpose by means of *smṛti* (traditional scripture) alone. The reason for stating the fruit is "as before," and so forth; [it was stated] for the sake of the previous Bhāgavatas and those learned in the three Vedas (*traividyāḥ*).

The meaning is that, just as the fruit consisting of the attainment of the Lord and the attainment of something other than Him has been stated—namely, "Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; My devotees go to Me also"—no such fruit has been mentioned for those who hate [Him]. "This is being stated" means that their lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of the Lord's essential form is now being explained. To the question, "By what reason are the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord designated by the terms 'the manifest' (vyakta) and 'the unmanifest' (avyakta)? he says: "As the Self of all. This refers to the previously mentioned convention.

The meaning is that the doubt mentioned in the introductory verse to the *śloka* is [here] intended. He himself clarifies the manner of dispelling that doubt with the words beginning "It is true. He clarifies its status as an intermediate cause with the words "at the time of creation. With the words "therefore it is said," the meaning is that the result is being stated.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. Regarding the phrase "by way of the context of the explanation already stated": this indicates that the meaning of the chapter is precisely the explanation just given; anything else is merely incidental. Thus, one should not entertain doubts regarding a division of the chapter based on its having multiple meanings. Regarding the phrase "the means for that": the meaning is "the means for recollection. To the question, "How is this much meaning obtained by the word 'attainment' (prāpti)? he says: "At the time of death," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of [the verse] beginning with": the word "of recollection" is to be supplied as the remainder.

The meaning of the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) refers to such passages as, "He is called Brahman, the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord (*bhagavān*)," and so on. The phrase "because it resides in the Blessed Lord alone" (*bhagavanmātravṛttitvāt*) implies the scriptural authority (*śruti*) such as, "That indeed is the supreme Brahman," and so forth. The phrase "in the context of *prakṛti*, etc. implies such passages as, "My womb is the Great Brahman," "By that [Brahman] as the heart," and "All beings are born from Brahman. The phrase "thus above" (*ityupari*) refers to this very chapter. He states the remainder in two places prior to the word "doubt" (*saṃśaya*).

And here, by the word "iti," the remainder of the sense is "born from the cognition" (pratītyā jātaḥ). Regarding the phrase "of the gradation" (tāratamyasya), the meaning is: "by this [question], who indeed are considered the most fit? Regarding the phrase "but in the present context" (prakṛte tu), the meaning is: "in the passage 'the supreme imperishable Brahman'. Regarding the phrase "by the word 'me'" (mām), the meaning is: "by the words 'me, together with the elemental and the divine'. Regarding the phrase "by this," the meaning is: "because attainment has been stated through the mention of their association. Regarding the phrase "by this": [the meaning follows].

The meaning is: by stating that the form known as *adhiyajña* (the sacrificial aspect) is an internal form residing within the bodies of all living beings for the sake of sustaining the literary work (*sāhitya*). The intention is that this [internal nature] is already obtained simply by the mention of "in the body" (*dehe*). "How is that stated? means: how is the answer to the question "What is the statement 'the imperishable is Brahman' (*akṣaraṃ brahma*)? provided? It means: "How is it the answer to the question 'Is it Brahman? "It is the impeller of the universe" means that the activities of the entire world proceed from it; that is to say, it is the impeller of the universe. "By stating the definition of the Blessed Lord" should be understood as occurring immediately after this very point.

"Because it is stated that [He] is non-different from the Blessed Lord. Thus, the sense is that since the Blessed Lord—who is non-different from the Adhiyajña—is described as possessing qualities such as being a poet (*kavitva*), it follows that the Adhiyajña, being non-different from Him, is likewise endowed with those same qualities. "Only the attainment of That occurs" means that only the attainment of another object (the Supreme) occurs. "Regarding *aprārabdha*": this means the destruction of accumulated (*saṃcita*) and future (*āgāmin*) karmas other than those already begun (*prārabdha*), and the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) of them respectively.

The meaning is that this is based on the sūtra: "Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-clinging and destruction of future and past [karmas] respectively. Regarding the phrase "by experience" (bhogena): the meaning is that this is based on the sūtra: "But by experiencing the others, he is then finally absorbed. Regarding the phrase "by this": it refers to the root text's statement, "because it has been so said. The meaning is that those whose minds are disciplined—those possessing direct realization—know That Brahman as all-pervading; they perceive its true nature. As for the question, "How then can it be said [otherwise]? [the answer follows].

The meaning is: how can it be said [that this is so] because it serves as a means for recollection at the time of death? The phrase "beginning from the abode of Brahmā" (*ābrahmabhavanāt*) is a restatement of the sense of that [text]. The point is that the abode of Brahmā situated in Satyaloka is above Janaloka. "By this" means: by this scriptural statement of Smṛti. "This is not incorrect" means: it is not the case that the statement "they do not return again from the abode of Brahmā" is incorrect. "[Birth] with little effort," etc. [is the meaning].

The meaning is that although there is an absence of birth and death in their entirety, they exist in part. Regarding the phrase "and of this sentence": because the sentence "up to the abode of Brahmā" has that same sense, it means that one returns again in part. Alternatively, regarding the sentence "from birth to birth, existence occurs," the meaning is that there is no primary birth in the form of complete generation. Regarding the phrase "consisting of two *parārdhas*": the lifespan of Brahmā is called a *para*, and [the period] consists of two halves of that.

The Śruti states, "They attain the light" (te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti). However, the Sūtra says "by way of the light and so forth" (arcir-ādinā). Since the words *arciḥ* and *jyotiḥ* have the same meaning, it is stated that [the soul] first reaches the light (*jyotiḥ*). He explains the remainder of the Śruti cited in the root-text with the passage beginning "He who thus... (*ya evam...*). The meaning of the passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) is "during the southern solstice" (*dakṣiṇāyane*), and so forth. The meaning of the passage beginning with "Or else" (*ato vā*) is "again, for the knower," and so forth. This reading, "of the sun and the moon" (*sūrya-candramasoḥ*), is based on a scribal error.

Because the form *sūryācandramasoḥ* would result [if the rule] *devatādvandve ca* were applied to form *ānaṅ*. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, what is the purpose of the statement in the Gītā that for a knower of Brahman to attain Brahman, death must occur during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*)? To this he says: "In this regard. This means: in the Gītā. "In this regard" means: that there is no restriction of time for the attainment of Brahman.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. He says [the following] for the purpose of establishing the inclusion within the six [categories]: "Thus, the remainder" (iti śeṣaḥ). He raises an objection regarding its immediate succession to the seventh: "And not thus" (na caivam). The meaning is: because it is intermediate, being separated by the eighth. "Knowledge" (jñānam) means that which is to be known is called the object of knowledge (prameya). "Because of being devoid of touch" (sparśarahitatvāt) means that since touch consists of the capacity for contact, there is no manifestation [of it] as in the incarnations of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. "Having touched" (spṛṣṭvā).

Having known that [object] through the sense of touch, as one knows Caitra and others on the ground and so forth, and having brought about the transfer of their respective qualities such as coldness and heat—this is the intended meaning. By the phrase "because of being supported by the elements" (*bhūtādhāratvāt*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the absence of residing in the elements (*bhūtasthatvābhāva*). Regarding the phrase "by the state of being a body" (*dehatvena*): it should be construed with the word "reason" (*hetunā*). The meaning is that there is a suspicion of insentience, namely: "The body of the Blessed One is insentient, because it is a body, like the body of Devadatta. "Both" (*ubhayam*) refers to the state of being a body and the sentience that constitutes a defining characteristic of the Blessed One.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For it has two meanings. He shows the analysis (*vigraha*) obtained by the phrase "and of this, later on," namely: "with reference to this. This [is the meaning].

The meaning is "the universe. Regarding the phrase "whose senses," the meaning is "he whose [senses] are these"; "senses" here refers to the eyes. [The objection is that] there is a contradiction with what has been stated [previously]. The point is that by describing the body as having the characteristics of the Lord (Bhagavān), its non-material nature (*aprākṛtatva*) would follow. Regarding the phrase "as previously stated": the meaning is that there is a contradiction with the statement made earlier in passages such as "the sustainer of beings" (*bhūtabhṛt*), which describes the body as being of that very nature. It is said that "disregard" (*avajñāna*) consists in the lack of respect for those who are not incarnations, such as the earth and other elements, and for those who are incarnations, such as Vedavyāsa, Paraśurāma, and others, due to their being treated with contempt and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "But the great-souled ones, having known [Him], worship [Him]," he himself explains that even the mere remembrance of the nature of that knowledge is to be included here, by means of the passage beginning with "distinct from everything. The word "as it truly is" (*yathāvat*) should be construed with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). "That exists" means that which is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*). "He bears a *dara*" means that he bears a conch shell (*śaṅkha*). "In this remembrance" refers to the remembrance of those respective objects. "The former [is] the supplement of the former."

The meaning is that this [verse] illuminates the fact that the meaning of the names "Arka" and so forth has already been stated. Otherwise, the word *evam* (thus) would be improper due to the absence of an object for such a reference (*parāmarśa*). The intention is that the author of the root text did not state it as a supplement to what preceded because it shares the same meaning as the previous Smṛti. He says, "Because it is dependent on that," indicating that independence and universal agency are not only the reasons for the statement "even one who is different," but are also the reasons for the statement "the respective name is thus spoken."

The meaning is that, because the grounds for the application of words depend upon Him—specifically because they depend on the Lord—the entire collection of words possesses their referents (arthavat), just as the forms of the Blessed One possess their referents, according to the logic stated in the Sūtra. Regarding the term "cause" (kāraṇam): the sense is that it is like a king being designated by the word "conqueror" (jayin) with respect to the victory achieved by his servant. He explains the meaning of "residing in the vital breaths" (prāṇagaḥ), "the sustainer of the vital breaths" (prāṇadhartā), and so forth, with the words "abiding in the senses," etc. To the inquiry "When does he dissolve the universe?", he says: "The remainder [of the sentence] is 'during the dissolution' (pralaye)."

To prevent the arising of doubt later on, he states that another meaning mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* should also be understood here: "I am the sacrifice" (*ahaṃ kratuḥ*). He says, "It is stated along with its cause. This means that the difference in results is stated to have as its cause the difference in the means of attainment, which consists in the manner of worshipping the Lord. He clarifies that very difference in the means—consisting in the manner of worship—which is the cause of the difference in results, by the words beginning with "another deity" (*anyadevatā*). "As stated" means as stated in the verse beginning with "by whom" (*yayā*).

"By being its counter-correlate" means by being its opposite. "Of what was stated" means of what was stated in the *Gītā*. "It is stated" means it is stated in the subsequent verse right here. "Desire has been mentioned" refers to the preceding verse; [the phrase] "even from a Vaiṣṇava" is an inference. "Bhagavat," etc., is the explanation. "In such passages as" refers to the *Vājasaneyi* and so forth. "And by the force of the word 'abhi'"—the sense is that this word carries the meaning of "perfectly" (*samyak*). "The rest is as follows" refers to the aforementioned passage.

The meaning of the phrase "I abide among them with affection" and so forth is as follows: "That very thing" means "I exercise affection only toward devotees. "As for the verse beginning 'The devotee who always... means "as stated in the Smṛti that will be cited in the eighteenth [chapter]. "By the word 'etcetera'" means "by the word 'sin and so forth'. "Sudyumna’s state of being Ilā" is clearly explained in the second [chapter] of the ninth Skandha, beginning with: "Due to the transgression of the Hotṛ priest, she became a girl named Ilā, who was not devoted to the Lord," and so on.

Regarding the statement "the Apsarases were the sons of Agni": this is made clear in the twentieth chapter of the *Bhāratatātparya*, in the passage beginning with "For they were formerly the sons of Agni" and ending with "born in royal families," which states that they attained womanhood through penance; and it is also clearly stated in the tenth chapter of the *Prathamaskandhatātparya* in the *Mahākaurma*: "The high-souled sons of Agni attained womanhood [and became] wives of the unborn, all-pervading Vāsudeva, the source of the universe. Regarding the phrase "of Ambā":

"She will be a male"—from this [statement] she was born as Ambā; from the passage beginning with "by name Śikhaṇḍinī" up to "he became Śikhaṇḍin by name," this is made clear in the eleventh chapter of the *Bhāratatātparya*. Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*): it means that superiority in this world and so forth is produced by limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as being born into a noble lineage. Regarding the phrase "and at another time": the meaning of the particle *ca* is that it is not merely a matter of [being a] boon (*vara*).

He says, "By way of restating what preceded," in order to dispel the doubt that there is a redundancy because it was previously stated that those who possess the *svābhāvya* (inherent nature) alone attain liberation. He says, "As being non-contradictory," which means: as being non-contradictory with the statement previously cited regarding *sattva* and so forth. He clarifies the meaning because it is difficult to understand, saying, "By this," which means: by the statement regarding those who perform sinful acts and so forth.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the glorious *Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. He states the subject matter of the chapter as explained in the Commentary: "In the sixth," etc. It should also be understood that what was reminded at the end of the ninth chapter—"Be one whose mind is fixed on Me"—is included here; thus, there is no room for the doubt regarding its immediate sequence to the sixth chapter. Although the object of meditation has been stated in various places, such as at the beginning of the fifth chapter in the words "the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities" (*yajña-tapasām bhoktāram*), nevertheless, with the intention that the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Lord are to be meditated upon by qualified aspirants, he says: "The manifestations of the Lord," etc. The meaning of the word *vibhūti* will be made clear later. "On account of being that [nature]," etc.

The meaning is "due to the existence of ignorance. Regarding the term *bhūta-bodha*: from the root *budh* (to awaken/understand), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). With that as its attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *ki* is applied to the root *dhā* (to hold) according to the rule *ghoḥ kiḥ*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding "the well-known Manus": the meaning is that those known as Svāyaṃbhuva, Svārociṣa, Raivata, and Uttama are the well-known Manus. Regarding "with the intention of referring to the castes such as the Brahmins": [this refers to the classification of beings].

The meaning is that the number four is intended because among the gods there are some who are Brāhmaṇas, some Kṣatriyas, some Vaiśyas, and some Śūdras. It should be understood that this fourfold classification is clearly stated in the first chapter of the Vājasaneyi-bhāṣya, beginning with the words: "From Viṣṇu was born the Brāhmaṇa caste, and Brahmā, the four-faced one," and so forth. By the phrase "by this very [statement]," the meaning is by citing the remainder of the Smṛti text beginning with "But Marīci and the others. The word "upeyam" means that which is to be attained.

In order to exclude the error of [interpreting the term] as the exclusion of anything else (*anyavyāvṛtti*), he first employs the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by abandoning the particle *eva* (only). "And power" (*śaktiśca*): the connection (*anvaya*) is with the word "yoga. "Capable" (*śakyam*): the meaning is "suitable for being the object of power. "And that has been stated": the meaning is that power has indeed been stated either by the mention of the creatorship of the elements and the elemental qualities such as intellect (*buddhi*), or by the explanation of the word "prabhava" (origin) as "prabhāva" (power). "They resort to it in that way": the meaning is either through faith in the knowledge of its being the cause of all things, and so forth.

Regarding "from one's own class, etc. (*svajātyādi*): this means "among things superior to one's own wife and so forth," that is, among excellent things. Since Indra (*Vāsava*) and others do not possess superiority over all the gods of their own class, and since the *Gītā* states that superiority can sometimes exist even over those of a different class, he says: "This is an illustration [of superiority] over a portion of one's own class, etc. The phrase "and so forth" refers to the remainder [of the argument]. Regarding the cause for the superiority [of the Sāman] over the Vedas, it is stated: "of the Sāman."

The sense is that [the word] "utkarṣahetuḥ" (cause of excellence) is used here in the form "of the aśvattha tree. Regarding the statement "the root *iṇ* in the sense of 'motion'": the sense is that from the root *iṇ*, with the prefix *rava-* as an upapada and the suffix *kvip*, there is elision of the final letter of the upapada, resulting in the form *raviḥ*. Regarding the statement "dwelling (*vāsaḥ*) is in all places": the sense is that the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *vas* in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Regarding the statement "it exists (*vartate*)": the sense is that the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *vṛt*. Regarding the statement "protectors (*pāḥ*) are those who guard": the suffix *vic* is applied to the root *pā* in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇa*). The word *mā* is a restatement (*anuvāda*), explained as meaning "there is not. Regarding the word "by itself (*svataḥ*)": [this is the sense].

The meaning is "from itself. Regarding the phrase "of the Chāndogya Śruti in the eighth chapter," the meaning is as stated. Regarding the phrase "Vainateya is related to that," the intention is that the suffix *uka* is used in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha*). Having accepted that the suffix *ika* is used in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), he says: "Vāsuki possesses that. He explains the purpose of using the word "makara" instead of saying "mākara": "It has the sense of 'deficient' (*ūna*). This is stated based on the root list which gives *auhāk* the meaning "to abandon" (*tyāga*); thus he says "they abandon" (*jahataḥ*), meaning "they renounce" (*tyajataḥ*). "They resort to" (*śrayante*)...

The root *śri* means "service," such is the meaning. Regarding *bṛhatsa*: the intention is that the word *sāra* undergoes the substitution [of *sa* for *ra*]. Regarding *iti dhāroḥ*: the intention is that from that [root], with the suffix *asun*, the form *uśanā* is produced. Regarding *munisaṃbandhī*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *muni* in the sense of a relationship; and the intention is that the relationship consists of the form of the praised and the praiser. Regarding *śīrṣasthānatvāt*: the meaning is "because of being the final point of attainment. He speaks having arrived at the form [of the word] from the root *ās* in the sense of "sitting."

"Āsā sthitiḥ" (The abode of hope). He states the meaning of the suffix -un (in *sthānun*): "Because of its nature as a support (*śīlatvāt*). He explains the meaning of the phrase "among rabbits and so forth, [He is] the owner distinct from others" and so on: "Among rabbits and so forth. The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes: "Of luminaries, the sun is the radiant one; of immovable things, the Himālaya," and so on. This was stated to establish His nature as the embodiment of sovereign power (*vibhūti*). He says: "By virtue of having the essence of *sattva* and the rest. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such passages as: "Of beings, consciousness is the essence; of those who restrain, self-control; of those who debate, the argument; and of those yet to be, their future arising," and so on.

"Is said": this should be connected with "the Blessed One. "Wherein [it is said] of the Sāmaveda": the meaning is that in the *Chāndogya* it is stated, "Of speech, the *Ṛgveda* is the essence; of the *Ṛgveda*, the Sāmaveda is the essence," and so forth. "'And so forth is what is said': the meaning of the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*) includes such things as 'when Śrī is the deity of the *Ṛgveda*, its excellence over all the Vedas,' etc. 'Without having said this': the sense is that because, by the force of the context, it is precisely the state of being presided over (*adhiṣṭhitatva*) that must be stated, the aforementioned [interpretation] is inconsistent. 'Even from that': [this refers to the subsequent argument].

The meaning is that, although [the Lord] has already been described by way of His characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), He speaks with even greater detail here by stating His pervasion of the universe. "The attainment of both" means that when there is the attainment of both—the previously mentioned limited manifestations (*vibhūti*) such as the Sun and so forth, and the nature of knowledge—there is the acquisition of something even more excellent.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.

Hari Oṃ. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of meditation" (dhyānārtham): since the meditation on the all-pervading form (*vyāptarūpa-upāsanā*), which was previously described in brief in the passage beginning with "I, having pervaded," cannot be easily accomplished because it does not readily descend into the intellect, meditation is only possible when that [pervasion] is heard in detail. Therefore, the meaning is that the state of the previously mentioned all-pervading form is now stated here in detail for the sake of meditation. By this, it is intended that its immediate sequence (*anantaratā*) to the preceding section is established. The phrase "previously and subsequently" means the connection between the prior and subsequent times.

Since three points to be established (*sādhya*) have been stated at the outset, [the author] asks, "By what is what established? and answers with the passage beginning with "Show," etc. "By this statement" means by the statement of the definition of the Lord (*bhagavat*), which consists in His possessing qualities such as playfulness (*krīḍā*). Having accepted that "my body" also connects with the preceding part, he says, "The winds likewise; my body. "Another supporting argument" means with respect to the possession of inconceivable sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). "Specified" means possessing particularity (*viśeṣa*). "And not there... [and so forth].

The meaning is that even though there is no difference between the particular (*viśeṣa*) and the particularized (*viśeṣin*), the conventional usage "this is the particular" and "this is the particularized" arises from other particulars. Regarding the phrase "the conventional usage of particulars": it means the conventional usage such as "this is a particular" and "this is a particularized. He provides the very same application [of this principle]: "In the case of the conscious [soul]," etc. Regarding "because of being the material cause of the particular": it means because of being the material cause with respect to the particular. The division [is made] by the words "even though it does not persist as long as the substance. Regarding "as an effect": it means in the form of the effect of a particular. Regarding "because it has been stated": [it refers to what was said previously].

The meaning is that nothing unspecified is intended by us, because this was already stated implicitly in the preceding sentence; or else, because it was stated in the second [section] with the words "Since the essential nature is already established, the scripture would be redundant," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because the qualifier excludes the qualified": the sense is that when it is asked to whom belongs this perceived qualified form—such as "this is blue," "yellow," or "staff-bearer"—the answer is given, "Caitra's" and so on. Regarding the phrase "in that qualified [object]": the meaning is "in that which is qualified by having the essential nature of the qualified object."

"In the event of its attainment" (*tatprāptau*) means: in the event of the occurrence of defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*). "The question is untenable" (*praśnānupapattiḥ*) means: the question "What is Caitra qualified by? is inappropriate. The meaning of "non-different" (*abhinnam*) is "its own nature" (*tatsvarūpam*). In the phrase "and because of infinite regress, etc. (*anavasthādeśca*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes three further defects: the lack of qualifiers for the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the unknowability [of that nature], and consequently, its non-existence. "And 'I'" (*ahaṃ ca*)—the word "another" (*anya*) should be supplied here. "As has been stated" (*yaduktam*)...

"In this context," it should be connected with the phrase "it is eternal even as a substantial entity (*dravyātmanā*). "It has been established" means that the absence of the experience "I am other [than Him]" has already been stated. "Of those eternally manifested" means those known together with their substratum (*dharmī*). "Appearance and disappearance" means those whose cognition is occasional. "Previously" refers to the fact that both difference and non-difference cannot be qualifiers of the agent and the enjoyer.

The meaning is that since the experience "other than me" does not exist at all, on the basis of this statement, identity is established by implication. "Of such things" means of those things characterized by manifestation and disappearance. "Both kinds of particularity" means particularity of both the natural and extrinsic (upādhika) types. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "of particularity etc.," specific causes are included. Thus, difference and non-difference have been stated.

By the statement that "those two, difference and non-difference, are not qualifiers of the agent and the enjoyer," it is meant that difference and non-difference are established by implication as qualifiers other than the qualifiers such as agency; thus, they are said to be "already stated" (uktaprāya), meaning they have been effectively established. Regarding the phrase "he supports" (*samarthayati*): since the ātmanepada suffix conditioned by the anudātta accent is known to be non-obligatory (*anitya*)—as indicated by the addition of the *ḍit* marker to the root *cakṣiṅ*—the form *samarthayati* is grammatically correct. For this very reason, there is the usage in the *Raghuvaṃśa*: "The beloveds entreat him who has risen from his bed. (*prārthayanti śayanotthitaṃ priyāḥ*).

The explanation of the word "ataḥ" (hence) is "ekaikeṣām" (of each one). This means: of either mere difference or mere non-difference. Now, an objection might be raised: since the question concerns the experience of difference or non-difference between the qualifier and the qualified in an insentient object, the mention of such an experience regarding the threads and the cloth is irrelevant; therefore, he connects that [example] as follows: "From the constituent parts, such as the threads..."

[This is explained] by the passage beginning with "ityādinā. The word "ekaikatantor" (of each individual thread) is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). He states himself what was not mentioned in the root text: "sarvāvayavasamudāyasya" (of the collection of all parts). Alternatively, this statement is made by taking the meaning of the phrase "different from the threads" (*tantubhyo'nya*) to be "those which have attained a particular configuration" (*saṃsthānaviśeṣāpannebhyaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "because of the lack of plurality" (*abahutvāt*): the sense is that if there were plurality, it would not be logical for there to be non-difference [of the cloth] from the cloth as the object of a cognition of unity. "In its existence" (*tadbhāve*) means in the existence of the collection. "The whole" (*avayavinā*) refers to the possessor of parts.

The point is that only those threads which have attained a specific configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*) and thus participate in the linguistic usage as parts can be considered the possessor of parts (*avayavin*). Why should there not be non-difference of the cloth even from each individual thread? What is the use of accepting their difference? Nor is it impossible for them to be non-different from a single cloth simply because they are many; [the opponent] raises this doubt by means of an illustrative example: "Just as [the qualities] residing in the Self... The phrase "of what was stated" means: of what was stated [by the opponent], namely, that there is absolute non-difference from the single cloth because [the threads] are not many. [The author replies: "Because it has already been stated."

The intended meaning is that this is the occasion for the explanation beginning with "Even though it is eternal as a substantial entity" (*dravyātmanā sa nityo’pi*). "In the ultimate composite alone" (*antyāvayavinyeva*) means in an object that does not initiate another substance. "Difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedau*): the sense is "with each individual part. "From the conventional usage of existence" (*bhāvavyavahṛteḥ*) means from the conventional usage of the existence of the blue color. "After destruction" (*vināśānantaram*): the meaning is that prior to the destruction of the blue color and so forth, there is both difference and non-difference [of the substrate] from the color; however, after the destruction of the color, there is absolute difference due to the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).

"Harer bahuvyavahāraviṣayatām iti" means "the state of being the object of various transactions," such as "known by the thousands" and so forth; the sense is that it is the object of a specific transaction characterized by being within the scope of a large number. "Ity uktatvāt" means "because it has been stated thus": "Wherever the absence of difference is established by a means of valid cognition, there indeed is what is called 'particularity' (viśeṣa). "Tathā sati" means "that being the case."

The sense is that, since the individual soul (*jīva*) and [the Supreme] are one, in order to avoid contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, one must abandon the attributes belonging to both; thus, because only the attributeless consciousness remains, supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*) would be impossible. Thinking that [the Lord] possesses a form distinct from the atoms, he says: "of infinite forms" (*anantarūpa*). "Tautology" (*punarukti*) means: by the very statement that it is "in the form of repetition" (*abhyāsarūpa*). "The supreme treasure" (*paraṃ nidhānam*) means: the highest support (*uttamāśraya*). The phrase "by me this is pervaded," etc., is the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). To this, it is replied:

The meaning is that it is stated in the *Gītā*. "Asau" (this) means the word "all" (*sarva*). "For the purpose of establishing what was stated by himself" means for the purpose of establishing what was stated in such passages as "the supreme abode" (*paraṃ nidhānam*). "Of the three worlds" is to be construed with "is stated by Arjuna. To the question "By whom is it stated?", it is said: "Having seen," etc.; this refers to the passage beginning with "that infinite happiness" (*sukham ātyantikam*) in the sixth chapter.

Since it is observed that [the effect] does not appear even when there is capability if an obstacle is present, he says: "when free from obstacles. It is stated in detail in the *Viṣṇudharma*, in the nineteenth chapter: King Purūravas said to the Aśvins, who had come to see his beauty, "I am currently smeared with oil; having bathed and adorned myself with ornaments, I shall return. At that time, my form should be seen. [The Aśvins replied: "Even while you, the lord of the earth, are still unadorned..."

“We shall indeed see you adorned later, accompanied by Saṃkrandana,” so said the Aśvins. The king quickly went outside, and they beheld every part of the monarch’s body, including his limbs and minor members. Having gazed for a long time at the king’s hair, forehead, arms, face, eyes, and other features, those two subduers of enemies said to the protector of the earth: “O King, having entered and bathed, you shall see us again, O Lord of Men, once your body is adorned with the ornaments appropriate to you.”

Thus addressed by the two Aśvins, the king entered his home, bathed, anointed himself, and adorned with garments, ornaments, and finery; he then approached the presence of the Aśvins. Upon seeing his appearance, the two of them laughed. When the king asked the cause of their laughter, they said: "Listen, O King, to the entire reason for our laughter. It concerns the momentary loss of your splendor arising from your very sight: the beauty you previously possessed when unbathed is not present now, even though you are adorned with ornaments."

The meaning is as follows: "O King, with our divine eye we behold the transformation of the body of both this [Yudhiṣṭhira] and that [Duryodhana], which brings about decay," and so forth. "Of Yudhiṣṭhira and the others" means of the five Pāṇḍavas and of Aśvatthāman, Kṛtavarman, and Kṛpa. "Not slain in person" is to be connected with the word "by the Blessed One. "From the root *dhā*"—the meaning is that the form *āyuḥ* (life-span) is derived from the root *dhā* with the suffix *uṇ*. "Thus *dhātuḥ*" (of the element).

Therefore, because the suffix *it* is present, the augment *num* occurs by virtue of being *idit*, resulting in the form "Indra"—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "he who acts is 'Ka'": this is the *ḍa*-suffix applied to the root *kṛ*. This connects with the statement that "only the word 'pratyuta' is mentioned. To the question—why is it not specifically stated that "it was seen by Indra's body," rather than using the speaker's expression "by one other than you" and so forth?—the author replies with the words "of Indra," etc. "The cited Smṛtis" means the Smṛtis beginning with "The universal form [was seen] first," and so on. "As has been stated" refers to what was previously mentioned.

This is to be connected with the beginning of this chapter. "Otherwise" is a restatement; "by nature" is the explanation. "Superiority" means excellence. "In the cited passage" means in the passage beginning with "But the distinction between the higher and the lower," and so forth. "As stated otherwise" means there would be a contradiction with what was said [elsewhere], such as: "Having seen the wonderful form, Brahmā first beheld the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa)," and so on.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the glorious *Gītā*, composed by Raghūttamatīrtha. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. "As previously stated" means as stated in the verse beginning with "one who performs my work," and so forth. By this, the immediate succession of this chapter from the preceding one is also indicated. The word "having doubted" (*sandihya*) should be construed with "performed" (*kṛta*) that follows; by this, the grammatical validity of the suffix *-tvā* (lyap) is established. The meaning of "for the sake of the second Śrī" is as follows. "For that very purpose" is the meaning of "Śrī for the singers. "Śrī for the instructors" is [the meaning of the same].

Having accepted the meaning as "dwelling toward Śrī" (śriyaṃ prati vasānāḥ) or "having stood covering her" (tām ācchādya sthitāḥ), he states the result: "upāsīnāḥ" (sitting near). The statement "they go" (yanti) is an expression of the meaning through a transposition of the verbal suffix (lakāravyatyaya). In the commentary of Padmanābhatīrtha, however, the meaning is stated as follows: "The Goddess Śrī bestows (dadhāti) prosperity (sampadam), wealth, and long life (vayaḥ) upon the worshippers; for the couple (mitadrau) sitting near Śrī, their well-striven-for (samidhā samīhītāni) truths come to pass."

In the *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, however, it is stated that "in *mitadrāu*" means "in the ocean" or "in the milk-ocean. The phrase "for what purpose is it performed? is to be understood as a question (*praśna*). By the word "by this" (*etena*), the meaning is: by the demonstration that the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) has consciousness (*cit*) as its material cause (*prakṛti*). He restates [the point] by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "from the meditation on the Unmanifest according to such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as... Now, an objection is raised: since the first and second halves [of the verse] concern the worshipper of Kṛṣṇa and the worshipper of the Supreme Brahman (*para-brahman*) respectively...

With the intention that Arjuna’s question is improper due to this distinction, [the author] objects: "Why is it untenable? He explains it as being "with a reason," meaning it is accompanied by the reason consisting in the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*). This will become clear later in the passage beginning with "Even for those of good conduct... and so forth. "Of those who are solely devoted to Śakti" means those who worship only the Goddess Śrī Devī while being devoid of devotion to the Lord and other such qualities. "Worship in the manner described" refers to the aforementioned way of service.

"Knowing her greenness" means that one who is devoted to her should meditate on Śrī after having worshipped Him (the Lord) in the manner previously described. "Even in deficiency" means even in the state of being inferior. "For this reason also" means for the reason that there is no delay, as in the case of the path of worshiping the Goddess Śrī, since the path of liberation consisting of the worship of the Blessed Lord has liberation as its fruit. "By two reasons" means by the two reasons of being without difficulty and not being delayed. After the word *iti*, which expresses the meaning of the reason, he states the remainder: "Of them," and so forth.

The meaning of "and" (*ca*) is that it is not merely the absence of afflictions (*akleśa*) and so forth. "Precisely as before" (*pūrvam eva*) means that it has already been refuted in the seventh [chapter] by such statements as, "But their fruit is finite" (*antavat tu phalam teṣām*). He restates the meaning of the four verses in brief with the words beginning "of my worship" (*mad-upāsanasya*). This is the citation of the opening words (*pratīka-grahaṇa*) of the four verses. Regarding "in me" (*mayi*) and "he becomes fit for union with that" (*tad-yogo bhavati*): the meaning is that he becomes fit to perform all actions through his Vaiṣṇava nature. "By this" (*tad anena*)... [refers to the aforementioned].

The meaning is that the passage beginning with "śreyo hi" [II.2.2] has been explained as being incorrect by means of the citation from the Smṛti. "Sannyāsaṃ tu" means "but renunciation" (tyāga). "Ayogataḥ" means "due to the absence of the performance of action. "Iti uktatvāt" refers to what was stated in the fifth chapter. "Prapañcyate" should be construed as "by stating other duties than those mentioned therein. "Anyathāpratītiḥ" means the impression of a general prohibition of undertaking [action]. [This is so] because it has already been explained by the Smṛti itself.

In the third [chapter], the sense is that there is an abandonment of the conceit "I am the agent" through the remembrance: "I am not the agent; Hari is the agent, as is the entire action of His worship. This is because it has been explained that the renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*) consists in the form of offering [the action] to the Blessed Lord, by means of [the statements] such as "Hari is the agent. Regarding the phrase "because it will be explained": the meaning is that it will be explained in the eighteenth chapter as a supplement to what was stated in the verse beginning with "having abandoned all duties" (*sarva-dharmān parityajya*). Regarding the phrase "as being non-contradictory to what has been said": [this refers to the fact that the present teaching does not conflict with previous statements].

The meaning is that, because the statement beginning with "non-Vaiṣṇava" (avaiṣṇava) is not contradictory, he explains the term "auspicious state" (śubhapada) as referring to knowledge, devotion, and detachment, rather than to inauspicious things. By this, it is stated that for one who is a Vaiṣṇava, these [knowledge, devotion, and detachment] are not [the only requirements]. "By way of being its means" (tatsādhanatayā) means by way of being the means for knowledge, devotion, and detachment; that is, excluding the undertaking of activities such as gathering *tulasī*, worshipping the Lord, and pilgrimage. "In the mention of incomplete means" (vyastasādhanakathane) means in the mention of partial or non-comprehensive means.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā-tātparya-ṭīkā*, composed by Rāghavendra Tīrtha. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. He explains the purport-statement (*tātparyavākya*) beginning with "That which was first... in accordance with the direction stated in the commentary on the passage beginning with "the knowledge, the object of knowledge, the field, the Person," and so forth. The phrase "in abundance" is used because it is also taught in such passages as "Many births of mine have passed. Regarding the term "the second": the word "hexad" (*ṣaṭka*) is to be supplied [to form "the second hexad"]. In the passage beginning with "But indeed, I...", the phrase "that which is the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*)" is to be connected with the beginning of the second chapter.

In this context, the intention is that the description of the nature of the individual soul (jīva) alone holds primacy, whereas the nature of the Lord (bhagavat-svarūpa) is mentioned for the sake of that [soul]. Regarding the word "field" (kṣetra): the meaning is that it refers to the abode of the Lord, where Hari dwells; thus it is said to be the place of residence. With the thought that if the word "saṃkṣepa" were taken in its abstract sense (bhāvārtha), it could not be placed in grammatical apposition with the supplied word "chapter" (adhyāya), he explains it as being derived in the agentive sense (kartari) and thus indicative of "demonstrating": "It demonstrates by way of summary; thus, it is the 'Summary of All Subjects' (sarvārthasaṃkṣepa)."

The meaning is that it is a demonstrator by way of abbreviation; the intention is that the status of agent is metaphorically attributed to the instrument. Regarding the phrase "is refuted": this should be construed with the thought that the statement regarding its being the "field" (kṣetra) is because it is useful for the Lord’s knowledge in the manner of being the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). The phrase "as will be stated immediately after [the verse] 'the aggregate is conscious'" should be supplied. The meaning is that it is designated by the word "aggregate" as being a single part among the modifications of the field. Regarding the phrase "of the verbal root": [it refers to the root *dṛś*].

The intention is that the form [is derived] by applying the *sārvadhātuka* designation to the *vic* suffix and the *śar* designation to the *kuṇ* suffix. Regarding "because it is to be moved, it is *īram*": the intention is that from the root *īr* (to impel), with the *ghañ* suffix in the sense of the object (*karman*), the form *īram* is established. Regarding "from the root": the intention is that from the root *kṣi*, with the *auṇādika* suffix *trap* in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the application of *guṇa*, the word *kṣetra* is established. Regarding "it is also connected later": this means it is connected before the verse beginning with "That divine mind... (*daivī tu sā matiḥ*). Regarding "by way of being its counter-correlative" (*tat-pratiyogitayā*): [this refers to the relationship between the two].

The meaning is: "by way of being opposed to that. "It is neither that" means the *Gītā* verse, "It is said to be neither existent nor non-existent," has been explained. "It is also an indication of action" means it should be understood that one performs the actions of all the organs of action as well. "By this" connects with the preceding phrase, "thus it has been explained. "This is the intended meaning of what was stated beginning with 'it'" means that it is stated that [the Self] resides in the heart by way of the dimensions of greatness and minuteness.

"Only because of what was stated before": the meaning is that this is well-known from the statement previously made that "the Blessed Viṣṇu is the Kṣetrajña. "Mental modifications" means [modifications] such as knowledge, desire, and so forth. He states two meanings for the word *vyartha* (meaningless): "it may be either meaningless or contradictory. The sense is that if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the Kṣetrajña, there would be a contradiction in stating that the Blessed One is the Kṣetrajña. He raises an objection with the words beginning "this... The word *vā* (or) should be supplied after "it is said" (*ucyate*).

In some places, the reading is exactly the same. Regarding the passage "And know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi mām*), the explanation of the meaning of the word *jña* (knower) is given by adopting the etymological derivation that "He is the field (*kṣetra*) and He is its knower (*tajjña*"), thus referring to the individual soul (*jīva*) as the Knower of the Field. Alternatively, one might interpret it as "Know Me as the Knower of the Field, the individual soul, and all fields," thereby restating the word "all fields" (*sarvakṣetra*) with the accusative case ending. The phrase "of the field" (*kṣetrasya ca*) restates the doubt. The expression "of the individual soul," etc., refers to this and other such constructions.

The meaning of the words "yojanām" (connection) and so forth is that the non-difference of the field (*kṣetra*) is expressed through the etymological derivation previously stated. He raises an objection: "He knows the field" (*kṣetraṃ jānāti*). "Of all this" means "of the entire intended object. "In the initial sentence itself" means "in the interrogative sentence itself. The syntactical connection is: "by the insertion of a word denoting the Lord (*īśvara*). "As separate sentences" means: "He who knows this" and "And Me, the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi mām*) are separate sentences. "Of the body beginning with the unmanifest" (*avyaktādiśarīrasya*).

The meaning is: "of this body" refers to the body whose nature begins with the unmanifest (*avyakta*), as stated in the passage "O son of Kuntī"; that is to say, it refers to the unmanifest and so forth designated by the word "body" through its etymological derivation (*yogavyutpatti*). "It perishes" (*kṣīyate*) means "it remains" (*sthīyate*); this is because the verbal root *kṣi* signifies both dwelling and going. [The objection] is untenable.

"May it be so. The sense is that transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is a resort for those who have no other way out. "Knowledge is said [to be the means]"—here, the word *jñāna* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), and thus refers to both the act of knowing (*jñapti*) and its instrument. To distinguish between what constitutes the instrument and what constitutes the act of knowing, he introduces the root text with the words beginning "But surely... (*nanu*). And [it is said] "nor here... (*na cātra*).

The meaning is that there would be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya; for if one intends "it does not have a beginning" (*ādimat na bhavati*) as "beginningless" (*anādimat*), then according to the root text's intended sense, it should simply be "beginningless" (*anādi*). Regarding the phrase "in that case": if one accepts the analysis (*vigraha*) "it does not have a beginning" as "beginningless," and thereby accepts the meaning "not possessed of a cause," then this meaning is already established by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, "that which has no beginning (cause)" (*na vidyate ādiḥ kāraṇaṃ yasya*). Consequently, the suffix *matup* would be redundant; such is the stated contradiction. Regarding the phrase "of what was said therein": [this refers to the aforementioned point].

The meaning is as follows: "possessing a beginning" refers to bodies, sense organs, qualities, and actions, which have a beginning because they possess it. "That which has no such things possessing a beginning" is what is meant by "beginningless" (*anādimat*); this refers to the primary sense of the term. Regarding the phrase "of the defect": it means the defect of the superfluousness (*vaiyarthyadoṣa*) of the possessive suffix *matup*. Regarding the phrase "having accepted that": having accepted the defect of superfluousness, he cites a purpose consisting in the removal of an objection—namely, that [the Self] is not its own cause—by relying on a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) such as "it does not have a beginning" (*anādi*), meaning it is not an initial cause.

The meaning is that [the self] takes up [the body] without attachment. Between the two meanings of the particle *ca*—namely, *anvācaya* (conjunction with emphasis) and *samuccaya* (simple conjunction)—it is the sense of *anvācaya* and not the sense of *samuccaya*. Even when "beginningless" (*anādi*) is stated, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—"that which has no initial cause"—the meaning obtained is "it does not have itself as its own cause. However, in the case of a *nañ-tatpuruṣa* compound, one must resort either to a Vedic anomaly regarding gender or to the elision of a case-ending; otherwise, since the word *ādi* is invariably masculine, the form would have to be *anādiḥ*.

Therefore, by means of the initial *na*, he accepts the attainment of the purpose—which consists in the removal of doubt—by way of non-attachment; thus, the analysis of the compound (*vigraha*) is resorted to. In reality, however, the intention is precisely the meaning stated in the Bhāṣya; this is the sense. "This very thing" (*etad iti*) means the collection of words beginning with "Supreme Brahman. "Because it has been stated" (*uktatvāt*) refers to the tenth [chapter]. "One who knows independently" (*svatantravettā*): the absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the rule that "the teaching of grammar is not absolute" (*āgamaśāsanamanityam*). It means "one who knows" (*veditā*). He states the previously mentioned meaning—"one who knows himself" (*svavettā*)—with the words "Sva is independent," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "knowledge is one's own" (*svam*), he says: "One's own (*svaḥ*) means independent (*svatantraḥ*)," and so forth. The phrase "to be known by oneself" (*svena vedyaḥ*) is a restatement of the aforementioned meaning. "One's own (*svaḥ*) means self-luminous (*prakāśaḥ*)" and so forth; the meaning is "one's own (*svaḥ*) means independent (*svatantraḥ*). And the sense is that [the suffix] *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), as in "he himself" (*sa ca svayameva*). "Cognition" (*vittiḥ*) is likewise a restatement of the aforementioned meaning. Regarding the phrase "and this is one's own (*svaś cāsau*)," etc., one might ask: why is the meaning already stated as "the knower of another" (*parasya vettā*) not explicitly mentioned here as "by others" (*paraiḥ*)? To this, he says: "The knower of another," and so forth.

However, in the manner previously stated, the word "attained" (*prāptam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis for the purpose of dispelling doubt. "Otherwise perceived" (*anyathāpratītau*) means "perceived as being of my own nature. He states the connection mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* with the words "Since... (*yataśca*), etc. "To speak" (*vaktum*) is to be construed with "as the overseer" (*upadraṣṭā*), etc. Therefore, the meaning is that whatever exists as the field (*kṣetra*), such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth, proceeds from the Impeller (*preraka*). Nor is it the case that [the Impeller] was not already proposed by the statement "And he who is the Impeller" (*yaśca prerakaḥ*). [The word "he"] is used in the masculine gender for the sake of grammatical coordination (*anvaya*).

The meaning is that, for the sake of connecting [the two], both terms denoted by the word *puruṣa* are mentioned first for the sake of their connection; having first stated the meaning of the word *puruṣa* mentioned later, the meaning of the word *prakṛti* is stated afterwards. To the question, "What is achieved by this out-of-order explanation? he says: "By this... [and] "as separate sentences. The meaning is: "Know both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—both as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), and know both as the primordial natures (*prakṛti*), sentient and insentient, and both as beginningless"—thus [it is]. And so, there is a summary.

The meaning is that this [term] is also included here. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "he refutes what is well-known. He raises an objection with the words: "of the material nature (*cit-prakṛti*), which is the cause of ignorance," and so forth. The syntactical connection is: "is the causality being stated in a qualified manner? The answer to this is made clear later by the passage beginning with "by this [power] of the Blessed One," etc. "By its own action" means "by its own operation. Or, for this reason he says "as follows" (*yathā*). The sense is that its meaning is exactly as before. He raises an objection with the words: "if the word 'puruṣa' is used here," and so forth.

"Merely by restating what has been said before" means: merely by repeating what was stated previously. He states the supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*): "of the internal experience of objects. "Only externally" means: only in cases such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. "Therein" means: because there is no evidence for the existence of a settled distinction based on worldly usage (*vyavahāra*). "In the absence of that" means: in the absence of establishing the distinction between error and non-error. "Also of the validity of scripture and so forth."

The meaning is: "of the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the knowledge produced by that [scripture] as well. Regarding the phrase "starting with 'ityādeḥ'": the meaning is "up to the end of the passage 'nothing whatsoever is established'. Regarding the word "sādhyā" (the probandum): the meaning is "insofar as it is intended to state the consequence (*āpādya*). Regarding the phrase "tatsvarūpaprāmāṇyayoḥ" (of its own nature and its validity): the meaning is "of the nature of the knowledge produced by the scripture 'vimuktaśca' and of its validity. Regarding the expression "itiśabdasyārthoktau": the meaning is "in this manner, when the meaning of the word *iti* is stated. Regarding the phrase "ityarthasādhakaśruteḥ": the meaning is "of the scripture beginning with 'vimuktaśca' which establishes this meaning."

"This was said having accepted [the opponent's position]" means that this was stated while accepting the principle that "the difficulty of establishing something through reasoning does not constitute a sublation of what is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "In that very context" implies the connection with the phrase "difficulty is not a sublation. "By the aforementioned method" means by the method stated starting with "if it were slightly conscious," and so forth. "Of the relationship between cause and effect" refers to the agency of cause and effect itself—as in "for the person (*puruṣa*) is situated in primordial nature (*prakṛti*)"—as well as the previously mentioned experience of pleasure and so on. "Thus" [concludes the point].

The meaning is: "according to the manner stated by the author of the *Tātparya*. Regarding the phrase "according to the manner stated": the meaning is "according to the manner stated [in the passage] beginning with 'For [there is no contradiction] between knowledge and ignorance'. Regarding the phrase "being situated in *prakṛti*": the meaning is "being endowed with a body and sense organs. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): the meaning is "the connection with a body in the state of being a living soul (*jīva*). In the phrase "possessing qualities" (*saguṇatvam*), the words "the cause of that" (*tatkāraṇam*) are to be supplied. Regarding the phrase "because of its impossibility": the meaning is "because of the impossibility of [attributes such as] having a body or possessing qualities. To this, he says [in response] regarding the claim that "that [body] exists as something illusory" (*mithyābhūtam*).

"Of that falsity" means: of the falsity consisting in the connection with the body and so forth. "Precisely as a reason" means: not as the meaning of the word [of the verse]. "By way of connecting with the word 'iti'"—it should be joined with the phrase "having the sense of a reason.
