"By the two aforementioned modes" means: by one's own intuition and by hearing from another. "A means other than meditation for them" means: having the form of one's own intuition and so forth. "The non-mention" should be joined with the verse beginning with "by meditation. "In such passages," etc.

The meaning is that this is stated in the commentary on the third quarter of the fourth chapter, based on the scriptural passage: "The gods indeed have internal light; the sages have internal light; humans alone have external light. The meaning is that [the author] states the means of valid cognition known as *pratibhā* (intuition). "He resumes the subject at hand" means that, in order to generate an intense desire for knowledge regarding the matter already mentioned—namely, "both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*"—he brings that subject back to mind by stating the result of such knowledge in the verse beginning with "He who knows him," and so forth. "Thus [it has been] explained" means...

"Explained here" means that which was stated in the *Smṛti* has been clarified. "And other characteristics thereof" means other characteristics of the deities belonging to the various levels (*bhūmi*) and classes (*jāti*). "Decreasing in sequence" means in the form of ninety-five, ninety-four, ninety-three, and ninety-two [yojanas], and so forth. This is the sense. "Of Sarasvatī and the others as well" [is the phrase].

The meaning is that Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, is the tongue; Śiva is said to be the *ahaṅkāra* (ego); and Upastha is that Śiva who is Manu and other such deities as previously mentioned. This is the meaning of the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*), namely: "the capacity to produce another effect. Regarding the phrase "by the aforementioned etymologies": this means by the etymology previously stated in the passage beginning with "and the cause of injury to the living being," etc. He states the meaning according to the direction given in the *Kāṇva-bhāṣya*: "But the deities, such as Earth and the rest, are like the body because they are under its control. This refers to the phrase "by being dependent on the Lord. The word "previously" (*pūrvam*) [refers to what was stated] before.

The previously mentioned Brahman alone, existing in the form of the agent, sets action in motion; action, however, is not the instigator of Brahman. This is because of the designation of Brahman’s agency and of action as its cause, as stated in the aphorism at the end of the *Bhaktipāda*: "By merit, He leads one to a meritorious world. Now, regarding the phrase "herein" (*nanvatreti*): this means "in the Gītā. After the words "herein also" (*atrāpi*), he completes the sentence by repeating "herein" (*atra*) and then states the meaning of the root text: "as far as... (*yāvaditi*).

"From association with that" means from association with *prakṛti*. The syntactical connection is "and this is not to be said. "Of this sentence-meaning" means of the meaning of the sentence beginning with "as long as," etc. "Enough" is to be construed as "sufficient for the human goals such as liberation. To ensure that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has the same meaning as its source (*mūla*), he states the intended meaning of the source: "of the elements," etc. "What was stated here" means what was stated in the sentence of the means of knowledge. "And the cognition of non-agency" means that it is not only the state of being the self of all [that is established], but also the removal of doubt.

Regarding the phrase "it does not become inert," he states the remainder by repeating the word "iti": "the remainder is 'iti vācyam' (it should be stated as such). He himself provides a corresponding illustration: "just as 'śūnya' (void)," etc. Relying on the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) of the word *mokṣa* as "that from which the liberation of beings [occurs] from primordial nature" (*prakṛti*), he says: "liberation and the means to liberation. To the question "What is that? it is said: "humility (*amānitva*) and so forth."
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. According to the method of the commentary, he states [the purpose] regarding the "subject matter" (*ghaṭṭārtha*): "By way of predominance" (*prādhānyena*). Here, by the word "means" (*sādhana*), one should understand that portion consisting of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—namely, the avoidance of desire and so forth—which pertains to the means for attaining knowledge of the Blessed Lord, such as ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), as described in the first six verses. It is said "by way of predominance" because the majesty of the Lord is also described in passages such as "My womb is the Great Brahman" and "The sun does not illuminate That. The sense is that this [term] is a comprehensive indicator with respect to abundance.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "By means of this chapter, he demonstrates [the truth] within the midst of the five chapters. Regarding the phrase "as stated": the meaning is that it is an exposition on the generation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) caused by the conjunction of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). He introduces the statement from the *Gītā* with the words "In the three qualities" (*traiguṇye*), etc. Regarding the phrase "established by such scriptural texts as the *Śruti*": the meaning is that by the statement in the *Aitareya-śruti* that the Sāman, the Supreme Self, and the Person (*puruṣa*) manifest preeminently [in the same locus], it is established that only one who is fit [for liberation] possesses the status of being the Person (*puruṣatva*).

"Following after" (*paretya*) is the restatement; "more than six" is the explanation. This means [more than] Jāmbavatī and the others. "Because of its possession of good qualities, it is called *sat*"—the sense is that it is stated: "The word *sat* is employed in the sense of existence. "It is a verbal root"—the sense is that with the suffix *asun*, it becomes *tamaḥ* (darkness). "In another sense"—this means in the sense of having exclusively the fruit of suffering, which is a different meaning from *rajas*; or else, it means in the sense of having only the fruit of knowledge for the wise, which is a different meaning from *tamas*.

"By means of the method for transcending the qualities (guṇas)," etc.: the meaning of the words beginning with "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) and "conduct" (ācāra). "Sādhviti": the meaning is "righteousness" (samyak-dharma). "Thus, the aforementioned meaning," etc.: the meaning is that even when one has attained the loss of worldly goals through the season of devotion to Viṣṇu, and even upon attaining the human goals (puruṣārtha) by abandoning them, devotion to Viṣṇu must still be practiced; such is the stated meaning. "Dīrghā vaiṣṇavī": the meaning is "to be practiced for a long time. He says, "Śrī is so called," because Śrī herself possesses the quality of goodness (sattva-guṇa).

"In both cases" means that one is said to have "transcended that" by abandoning the bondage created by it and by attaining something superior to it. He clarifies this with the words "just as. The construction is "only one [state] remains at the end. The meaning is that it remains at the end because it is the most excellent of all.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Śrī-Gītā-tātparya-ṭīkā-bhāva-dīpa composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. Regarding the phrase "the nature of the world" (*jagatsvarūpam*): the meaning is that the nature of the world has been described as consisting of the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *prakṛti*, *mahat*, and *ahaṃkāra*, characterized by desire and aversion—that is, accompanied by the modifications of desire, aversion, and so forth—and possessed of deities. To avoid contradiction with the commentary which states that [this] "shows the nature of transmigratory existence" (*saṃsārasvarūpaṃ darśayati*), he says: "of that very [world]" (*tasyaiva*). The sense is based on the etymology: "that by which one transmigrates" (*saṃsarati anena*). "Desiring to abandon" (*jihāsatā*) means desiring to cast off [transmigratory existence]. "Has been defined" (*nirūpita*)... [end of fragment].

The meaning is that by the passage beginning with "He who thus knows the Puruṣa," there is the means consisting of the knowledge of the Blessed One and so forth. "By being a part of that" means by the absence of being a part of that. "Because dharma and artha have kāma and mokṣa as their purpose" means that dharma has mokṣa as its purpose, and artha has kāma as its purpose. "The *aśvattha* tree stands like a horse": the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *supi*. "Why? [is asked].

The meaning is: "From what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? "Seeking the Blessed One" means having the form of hearing [the teachings] and so forth. Regarding the phrase "abiding in primordial nature" (prakṛtisthān), he says "abiding in the body" (śarīrasthān), accepting that the word *prakṛti* here refers to its effects. He states the meaning of the word "of all" as "by way of being the support. By this, the intention is that [the name] is "Vaiśvānara" with the long vowel according to the rule *nare saṃjñāyām*, and [the word] is "pūpam. [This concludes the section] "from the verbal root."
The intention is that the form "kṣara" is derived by adding the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) in the sense of "that which flows out through the door of the body."
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati. || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. Both of these are described in this chapter. By this, it is indicated that this chapter follows the previous one, because while in the preceding chapter the means to the two human goals—knowledge and liberation—were briefly stated in such passages as "those whose delusion is destroyed," and the obstacles to those human goals were briefly stated in such passages as "even though they strive, those of unrefined self," those characteristics consisting of the divine and the demonic are here elaborated upon. The word "therein" (tatra) means in the chapter devoted to stating the characteristics of the divine and the demonic. The phrase "by the mere remembrance of that" [is explained as follows].

The meaning is: "the collection of statements that have been cited. By the words beginning with "satī," he clarifies the contradiction with the *akṣa* (senses) and the contradiction with his own statement. "Satī" means "having the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*). The phrase "because even the falsity of everything is false" means that when it is said "everything is false," since the falsity of that [everything] is also included within the referent of the word "everything"—just like the world consisting of ether and so forth—the implication is that it falls within the scope of the term "all. The phrase "it is divine" means "this is the divine wealth for liberation. The phrase "being the cause of blinding darkness" [is explained as follows].

Precisely because the rule for adding suffixes at the end of compounds is not universal (*anitya*), the compound-ending suffix [ṭac] was not applied in the case of *samandhebhyas*. Therefore, one should not suspect that the form should instead be *andhatamasam*. The phrase "residing within the results of both of those" means that they possess neither such auspicious nor inauspicious results. Alternatively, the meaning is that because they possess the results of both, they are already included by the very mention of gods (*deva*) and asuras. [This explains the phrase] "even of the gods and so forth."

The meaning is: since even the gods and asuras have gone to darkness (*tamogati*), what distinction is there among the gods from the asuras? Or rather, the meaning is: since the gods, Gandharvas, and so forth have gone to liberation (*muktigati*), what distinction is there among the gods from the Gandharvas and others? Likewise, since even the lowest of humans have gone to darkness, the meaning is also: what distinction is there among the asuras from the gods? "As it was stated" refers to the sense that this was expressed by the word "those who go to liberation. "The statement regarding their natural disposition" (*nisargatva*) [is mentioned].

The meaning is that this is the statement regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatva*). "The absence of being otherwise" means the absence of change (*anyathātva*). The word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while "of the gods" (*devānām*) and so forth is the explanation. And as for the "purport" (*tātparya*): the meaning is not only the removal of the doubt as to why they are not to be grieved for, but also [the establishment of their immutability].
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. Regarding the phrase "and of performance and abandonment," it is to be construed with the word "impossibility" (asambhavāt). Now, one might object: when the question was asked, "What is the steadfastness (niṣṭhā) for those who cast aside the scriptural injunctions? it should have been answered simply by describing its sattvic nature and so forth. Why then is it described as being "threefold" and so on? To this he replies: "In response to that very question. Since steadfastness belongs to those who do not know the scriptural injunctions, and because such ignorance can manifest in three ways—sattvic and so on—it is impossible to describe the distinctions of sattva and the other qualities through the medium of that ignorance itself. Thus, the threefold nature is stated.

With the intention that there is no inconsistency—since faith, which was previously described as a constituent of sacrifice by way of being a qualification of the sacrificer, is now analyzed, and on the basis of its locus, their nature as *sāttvika* and so forth is stated; thus this [following] answer is appropriate to that question—he introduces the subsequent verse while explaining its status as an answer with the words beginning "Therein" (*tatra*) and ending with "becomes" (*bhavati*). The meaning of the verse beginning with "threefold" (*trividhā*) has been stated. The meaning of the verse beginning with "Whatever one's faith" (*yo yacchraddhaḥ*) is stated in the passage beginning with "Therein" (*tatra*). [The phrase] "that knowledge" (*taj-jñānam*) [is explained as follows].

"Knowledge of [the qualities] such as *sāttvikatva* (being characterized by *sattva*)," etc. "Of that which was stated" means of that which was stated in the fourth quarter [of the verse]. "Previously indeed" refers to the thirteenth chapter, beginning with the words, "The *satva* is sometimes called the individual soul (*jīva*)," and so forth. "Because of having multiple meanings" means because it has been stated that the suffix *mayaṭ* has three senses: in the sense of identity (*tādātmya*), in the sense of modification (*vikāra*), and in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). "That" means the *śraddhā* (faith) of the *sāttvika* type and so forth, which is to say, the sacrifice performed by those possessing *sāttvika* faith and so forth. "By this explanation," etc.

Regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): when it is stated that one who possesses *sāttvika* faith and so forth is "sāttvika," etc., the meaning is that this serves as an explanation for the inquiry as to what constitutes *sāttvika* faith and so forth—namely, that one who sacrifices to the gods and others possesses *sāttvika* faith and so forth. The phrase "in the same way" (*evam*) means that one should understand that *sāttvika* [faith] also belongs to the *tāmasa*, and likewise *rājasa* [faith] also belongs to the *sāttvika*, and so on. The intention is that in both cases, the phrase "consisting of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇātmikā*) should be understood as being supplied from the root text. The mention of "one who sacrifices with a mixture" (*vyāmiśrayājinaḥ*) is a restatement; the subsequent passage beginning with "out of sequence" (*akrameṇa*) is its explanation.

"Those performing the sacrifice" means those engaged in the act of sacrificing. "Not so"—this is the meaning of the phrase "not all," which begins with "akhilam. "In some cases, such statements" means that in certain texts, the explanation of the usage of expressions such as "Adhyakṣavidyā eats," "The gods eat," and "Śiva, Skanda, and others eat" is thereby provided. "By this" means by the passage beginning with "even having abandoned what is prescribed by the scriptures. "Due to the suspension of scriptural injunctions and so forth" means due to the ignorance or knowledge of scriptural injunctions.

"Regarding the statement of being the instigator (*prayojakatva*)," the sense is that this is expressed in the *Gītā* by the verse beginning with "threefold" (*trividhā*). "Knowledge of that" (*tajjñāne tajjñānam*) means that through knowledge of the sattvic and other types of faith, there arises knowledge of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as sattvic and so forth. "Sattvic-ness and so forth" means it should be understood that sattvic-ness is excellence (*uttamatva*), rājasic-ness is mediocrity (*madhyamatva*), and tāmasic-ness is inferiority (*adhamatva*). "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) is the restatement (*anuvāda*), while "of the syllable *oṃ*" (*oṃkārasya*) and so forth is the explanation. Thus it is established.

How is this known? To this he says: "by the force of the context" (*ukti-prasaṅgāt*). The meaning is that it is understood through the power of the topical discussion. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of *rasa* and so forth," he explains the meaning of the word *rasa*: "*rasa* means *rasāyana* (elixir). The sense is that just as in the root text the qualification "suffering, grief, etc. is cited as an indicator for the rule that pungent tastes and the like belong to *rajas*, so too for the rule that sweet tastes and the like belong to *sattva*, the qualification "longevity, etc. should be cited as an indicator.

And thus, the sense is that it should be understood that while [qualities] such as pungent taste are not causes of suffering, grief, and so forth—just as they are not causes of the quality of *rajas*—they are likewise not causes for the increase of longevity and other benefits, and therefore they do not possess the quality of *sattva*. [The author] raises an objection: "Not here, this... and so on.

"Even though it has not arisen" (annotpannatvepi): the sense is that by the word "it increases" (vivardhate), one hears that *sattva* has arisen from that [source]. Having accepted that the word *yāma* ends in the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an object (*karman*), he says: "*yāmaṃ yāmyam*" (the Yama [deity] of the watch). "Therein" (*tatra*): the meaning is "in the sacrifice" (*yāge*). "By another statement" (*vākyāntareṇa*): the meaning is by another statement such as "Oṃ tatsat" or "That which belongs to Viṣṇu," etc. "By that statement" (*tadvākyena*): the meaning is that this statement—the statement from the *Gītā*—is an exposition of the previously cited *smṛti* statement. And "that word" (*tacca padam*)...

The word "sat" has the meaning of "consciousness" (citi). "It becomes manifest" means that because of its connection with the Blessed One whose names begin with "Oṃ," even sacrifices and other rites bear that same name; thus it is said to be "manifest. "Upon its utterance" means upon the utterance of the syllable Oṃ. "For by that [it is] a mantra" means it is a mantra because it protects (trāti) the knower (maṃ). From the root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring," the form "ma" is derived either with the agentive suffix *aṇ* or with the suffix *ap*.

The form *mantra* is established by adding the suffix *ka*—according to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*—or the suffix *ḍa* to the root *traiṅ* (meaning "to protect"). In this very way, the connection (*saṅgati*) with the chapter is indicated. The meaning is that the connection within the chapter is based on the intended purport (*tātparya*): that action performed without desire for fruit and so forth is real (*sat*), while other [action] is unreal (*asat*).
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the *Gītātātparya* composed by Rāghavendra Yati. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. "The means for achieving the goals of human life" (pumarthasādhana) means that [the Gītā] has stated, in such passages as "The Vedas have the three qualities (traiguṇya) as their object," that it is the means for the knowledge which is the cause of liberation. "Traiguṇya" means the effect of the three qualities, beginning with sattva. "Neither fire nor sacrifice," etc., refers to the scriptural statement cited in the commentary on the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*. The opponent, ignorant of the underlying intention, objects: "Of the renunciation of action... [This objection arises] because of the contradiction with what was stated [in the Gītā]: "One should perform action alone."

The sense is that, since attachment has been stated to pertain to wholesome action (*kuśala-karma*), and aversion is understood to pertain to unwholesome fruit (*akuśala-phala*). [The question] "Is it for him in every way? means: does that binding action not lead to bondage for him in every way—that is, in its entirety? "For those who have renounced everything" means for those who have renounced the fruits of all actions. "Precisely because of renunciation" implies the ellipsis "of the fruit of action. "Even that" refers to one who has renounced the nature of actions performed out of desire for the sake of others.

And thus, by the statement "of the renunciants" (*sannyāsinām*), the sense is that it amounts to saying "of those who have renounced" (*tyāginām*). Regarding the phrase "even the relinquishing of attachment to action": the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that *saṃnyāsa* is not merely the abandonment of optional rites (*kāmyakarma*). "That knowledge is praised" means the knowledge of agency as spoken of in relation to one's own self. Having raised the objection of redundancy by taking the meaning of "he does not kill" (*na hanti*) in the root text to be "he does not entertain the thought 'I kill'" (*hanmīti bhāvam na karoti*), [the author] refutes it by supplying the missing words.

"It is said that he does not kill" refers to the reason [stated] therein. "It is a redundancy" should be connected with the phrase "the state is not produced by the ego-sense" (*nāhaṃkṛto bhāvaḥ*), because that [state] has already been accepted. The meaning is that the non-difference between the qualified and the qualifier has been accepted. "Devadatta is the knower" means "qualified by the property of being a knower"; "Devadatta" is the mention of the substantive. He applies this to the subject of the illustration: "In the same way, in the case of the Lord."

The meaning is that because the verbal root *aṇ* (in *aṇa paṇa gatau*) is etymologically [treated] as such, there is no lengthening of the vowel, but rather the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). "By means of sattvic knowledge and other instruments" means that since sattvic knowledge, its core principles, and so forth are the means to liberation, the distinctions among sattvic knowledge and the rest—caused by the [three] qualities—are stated for the purpose of practicing those means to liberation consisting of sattvic knowledge and the like. "Thus" is a restatement; "of the all-pervading" is the explanation. "The intention of the locative case" refers to this.

The sense is that since the state of being a substratum (*ādhāratva*) is based on difference, distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is thereby obtained. Regarding the phrase "it is called 'becoming' (*bhavati*) and 'insentient' (*jaḍa*"): the meaning is that because the root *bhū* signifies "existence" (*sattā*), even insentient matter—which begins with its own nature—is grasped by the word *bhūta*, as it possesses the form of "being. Regarding the phrase "because it has been stated": the sense is that this was already stated in the previous verse beginning with "among those divided," etc. By this, the *Smṛti* passage beginning with "if [it were]" is explained; the meaning of the explanation lies in the portion beginning with "the state of being all-pervading" (*sarvagatatva*). He states the meaning of the term "of the one" (*ekasya*).

"Of any one whatsoever" means of a single individual. "By way of having different substrates" means by way of having distinct and non-distinct objects. Regarding the word "vidhāya" (having performed), it should be connected with the third chapter. In the phrase "from the knowledge of the true nature [of the Self]," he completes the ellipsis: "it is known as being required," which is how it connects. He explains the manner in which that meaning is obtained with the words "I am the Supreme, the best of all," and so forth. "Even the agent" means even one who possesses the impulse conducive to action.

"If *dhṛti* (fortitude) is indeed devoid of deviation," means "devoid of stumbling. Regarding the phrase "because action is their additional [attribute]," he completes the ellipsis by repeating the word "stable" (*sthāyika*). "Additional" is to be connected with "in sequence. "That" means "the addition of action. "In such passages as" means "in this very subsequent verse. "Of those ending with the householder" means "of those ending with the householder as stated in the passage 'the lifelong student and the householder'."

The meaning of "non-creation" (*asarga*) and so forth is "the non-production of offspring" and so on. The phrase "the nature of the Brāhmaṇas and others has been stated" means that this was stated by the passage beginning with "Brāhmaṇas are *rājasa-sāttvika*," etc.; such is the intended sense. "It is to be understood thus" means that otherwise there would be a contradiction with subsequent statements such as "there is a superiority of the others," etc.; such is the intended sense. "Due to the absence of qualities" means due to the absence of qualities such as *sattva* and so forth. "In the manner already described" means determined by the manner stated in passages such as "only the superior [ones] are progressively [superior]," etc. "They are so called" [refers to the aforementioned].

The meaning is that in the previously cited Smṛti, those who are *sāttvika* among the *tāmasa* types are called "the lowest of men. "By two statements" means by the two statements: "But the *rājasa* are the demons there" and "But those who are *bhāgavata*. "By the manner previously stated" means by the manner stated in [the passage] beginning with "But the *śuddhasattva* are the *paramahaṃsas*. "By another statement" means by the other statement [beginning with] "But those who are *bhāgavata*. "Because it has been stated that they bestow their own fruit" refers to the fourteenth chapter.

"Rājasasāttvikādi" means those such as the *paramahaṃsa* and others; this is the meaning of the word "ādi" (and so forth). "Narādhamādi" means those such as the *daityas* and others; this is the meaning of the word "ādi. "Same" (*sama*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while "eka" and so forth is the explanation (*vyākhyā*). He states the established conclusion (*phalita*): "The ignorant" (*ajña*) means one who is devoid of both knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). "The purpose" (*prayojana*) refers to "the state of being" (*bhāva*); that is, "by means of the state of being" (*bhāvena*). "Of them" (*teṣām*) means "of those Kṣatriyas regarding whom superiority is spoken of. "It is to be seen as such" (*ityādi draṣṭavyam*)—so it should be understood.

"If he possesses qualities equal to a Kṣatriya, he is a Kṣatriya"—this is the meaning of the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*). Regarding the term "that and that": the sense is that one should understand it thus: "if he possesses qualities equal to a Kṣatriya, he is a Kṣatriya; if he possesses qualities equal to a Vaiśya, he is a Vaiśya," and so on. Regarding the phrase "only in the context of describing those respective duties": the sense is "only in the context of describing the duties of a Kṣatriya. Regarding the phrase "by the aforementioned reasoning": [it refers to] these qualities.

The meaning is: "by the method stated in [Manusmṛti] 10.83 and following, they are slightly inferior"; or alternatively, "by the method stated in [Manusmṛti] 10.97 and following. In the root text (*mūla*), the specific duties of the Kṣatriya have been stated; for the others, he states them himself: "In this way, agriculture and so forth," etc. The phrase "because service is the duty of all" implies that teaching is also a form of service, according to the direction already mentioned. The phrase "and so forth" means: fleeing out of fear for a Kṣatriya, and likewise the transgression of proper conduct for a Vaiśya, and so on.

"Regarding 'and so forth' (*ityādi*): the meaning is that one should contemplate that for a Kṣatriya there is non-retreat through fortitude, and for a Vaiśya [non-retreat] through righteous means such as agriculture, and so on. Regarding 'of what was stated': the meaning is 'of what was stated [in the verse], "even though not by nature" (*anisargataḥ*)'. Regarding 'no contradiction with what was stated': the meaning is that there is no contradiction with what was stated [previously], namely, that this is a specific duty for the Kṣatriya. Regarding 'he states the exclusion of this': the meaning is that he states the exclusion consisting in the fact that this must be performed by Kṣatriyas alone."

[Objection: But if Brahmins also possess the capacity to perform instruction (*śikṣā*), does this not contradict what was stated previously—that [the capacity] belongs specifically to the Kṣatriya? To this, he says: "In all these cases. He connects the two verses as a single syntactical unit with the words beginning "If [it were] for the Kṣatriya... [He explains] "as a means for attaining the perfection of actionlessness" (*naiṣkarmyasiddhisādhana*) to mean: in the exposition of the means for destroying all other adverse karmas (*ariṣṭakarman*) except those already begun (*prārabdha*). [He explains] "and there is no over-extension" (*na cātiprasaṅga*) to mean: that there is no contingency of knowledge increasing even in the state of liberation (*mukti*).

Regarding the phrase "in the attainment of Lakṣmī": by this, the meaning of the expression *brahmabhūyāya* (for the sake of becoming Brahman) is stated to be for the purpose of attaining Lakṣmī. Furthermore, by the statement "after knowledge," the sense that *naiṣkarmyāya* (for the sake of freedom from action) means liberation (*mokṣa*), and that *siddhim* (perfection) refers to the perfection of the knowledge of its means, is also indicated. Regarding the phrase "is distinguished": the meaning is that in the verse *svakarmaṇā tamabhyarcya*, he states some qualification regarding the performance of one's own duty. Regarding the phrase "in such passages as before": this refers to the second chapter. [The reason is] "because there can be no alternative regarding a reality."

The meaning is that since there can be no doubt regarding the reality of Hari’s being the supreme among all, the status of the *bhāgavata* as the most excellent does not apply to the *traividya*. "That too" means even the supremacy of the Blessed Lord. "State" (*bhāva*) means contemplation (*bhāvanā*). "Having promised" refers to the ninth chapter. Since no conclusion is seen in the verse beginning with "These two," he says: "Because of the remainder of the sentence. "Because it was stated previously" means in the beginning of the fourteenth chapter. "Conclusion of the means" [is the phrase].

The meaning is that a brief mention for the sake of understanding the ascent [to the higher stages] would be useless; otherwise, there would be the postulation of a different meaning. The meaning is that the explanation would be to abandon such attributes as "meditating on Me" and so forth. This refers to the state of having a single purpose (*ekārthatva*).

It has been stated that one should see that the identity of meaning is evident: by the phrase "always" (*sadā*) up to "that mind," the state of being the supreme among all is shown; by "endowed with love" (*premayukta*), the sense of "my devotee" (*madbhakta*); by "surrendering everything" (*sarvatra samarpaṇam*), the sense of "worshipping me" (*madyājī*); and by "the threefold uninterrupted worship" (*akhaṇḍā trividhā pūjā*) and so forth, the sense of "bowing to me" (*māṃ namaskuru*). Regarding the word "will be indicated" (*lakṣyate*): it means it is conveyed through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), i.e., the qualified person (*adhikārī*) endowed with qualities such as austerity (*tapas*) is being described. Regarding the phrase "from the commentary on the Gītā, etc. (*gītāvyākhyānādīti*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), study and hearing are included. Regarding the phrase "being the cause": the sense is that they are the deities (*devas*) because they impel all the sense organs. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means the manner in which [He] is established as being full of all qualities, as the giver of faultless bliss, and as the most beloved of the best of knowers—either in the *Gītā* itself or in the treatise titled *Tātparya-nirṇaya*. Regarding the phrase "he said that": it means he stated His own nature as the third incarnation of Vāyu. Regarding the phrase "that very one": [it refers to Him].
The meaning is that it is exactly in the manner established in his own work that he [attains] Hari.
Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is far removed from all defects, who is filled with divine hosts,
the lord of Śrī’s life-breath, and the bestower of the desires of his devotees.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Bhāvadīpa*, a commentary on the purport of the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā*, composed by Rāghavendra Yati. || 18 ||
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
